en: The section concerning Yājñavalkya begins with the words, "Janaka, the King of Videha," and so forth.
Although this does not differ in its subject matter from the preceding Madhu-kāṇḍa—since that too is primarily concerned with establishing the truth—it is not a mere repetition;
for the Madhu-kāṇḍa is primarily based on scriptural authority (āgama), whereas this section is primarily based on logical reasoning (upapatti).
For indeed, scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*upapatti*), when applied to reveal the oneness of the Self, are capable of showing it as clearly as a bilva fruit held in the palm of one's hand.
For it has been said: "It is to be heard and it is to be reflected upon.
Therefore, this section belonging to Yājñavalkya, which emphasizes reasoning, is commenced for the purpose of determining the very meaning of scripture through prior investigation.
The narrative (ākhyāyikā), however, is intended either for the purpose of praising wisdom or for prescribing a means [to that end].
For giving is recognized by the learned as a well-known means, and it is seen in the scriptures;
by giving, living beings are won over.
Since abundant gold and the gift of a thousand cows are obtained here,
a narrative has been commenced by means of another treatise for the purpose of demonstrating the means of acquiring knowledge and the giving of gifts.
Furthermore, association with those who possess that knowledge and engaging in debate with them is seen in the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*) as a means of acquiring knowledge.
And this is demonstrated with particular force in this narrative;
moreover, the increase of wisdom through association with the learned is directly perceived.
Therefore, the narrative is intended solely to demonstrate the means for attaining knowledge.
Janaka of Videha performed a sacrifice at which abundant sacrificial fees were distributed.
There, the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas had gathered together.
Now, Janaka of Videha desired to know: "Who among these Brahmins is the most learned?
He enclosed a thousand cows; ten gold pieces were tied to each pair of horns. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1.
There was once a king named Janaka, a sovereign ruler of the Videhas; he was thus called Vaideha because he resided there.

He performed a sacrifice known as the Bahudakṣiṇa—either a sacrifice well-known in other Vedic branches or the Aśvamedha itself, which is here termed "Bahudakṣiṇa" due to the abundance of sacrificial fees—with which he sacrificed.

At that sacrifice, Brahmins from the lands of the Kurus and Pañcālas, who were either invited or desirous of seeing him, gathered together; for it is well known that there is a great abundance of learned men among them.
They were present there.

Having seen that great assembly of learned men, a desire to know—who indeed here is the most proficient in Brahman (*brahmiṣṭha*)—arose specifically in Janaka Vaideha, who was performing the sacrifice. This was his wish to investigate.

"How? Who indeed among these Brahmins is the most learned (*anūcānatama*)? For all of them are learned; who among them is pre-eminently learned? Thus, having conceived a desire for knowledge regarding the one most learned in Vedic study, he—seeking a means to ascertain that—confined a thousand cows of the first age in a pen, causing them to be penned up.
It is now stated what kind of cows were thus confined.
A *pāda* is one-fourth part of a *suvarṇa*.
Ten *pādas* each were fastened to the two horns of every single cow;
that is, five *pādas* on each horn. //1//
He said to them: "Venerable Brahmins, let him among you who is the most proficient in Brahman drive away these cows.
But those Brahmins did not dare to do so.
Then Yājñavalkya said to his own pupil: "My dear Sāmaśrava, drive these [cows] away! He drove them away. Thereupon, those Brahmins became enraged.
"How might the one most devoted to Brahman among us speak?
Now, Āśvala was the Hotṛ priest of Janaka of Videha.
He questioned him: "Are you indeed, Yājñavalkya, the one most devoted to Brahman among us?"
He said, "We pay homage to the one most proficient in the Veda; we are merely seekers of cattle.
Then the Hotṛ Āśvala resolved to question him right there.

Having thus penned the cows, he said to those Brahmins: "O venerable Brahmins," thus addressing them, "he among you who is the most learned in the Veda (*brahmiṣṭha*)— for all of you are indeed Brahmins— he who is the most excellent Brahmin among you, let him drive these cows away toward his own home."

Those Brahmins, having been addressed in this manner, did not dare; indeed, they became neither bold nor confident enough to claim for themselves the status of being most proficient in the Veda (*brahmiṣṭha*). When the Brahmins had become disconcerted, Yājñavalkya then said to his own pupil, a *brahmacārin*: "O gentle one, O Sāmaśrava—so called because he listens to the rules of the Sāman—he who is Yājñavalkya, the knower of the four Vedas—drive these cows back toward our home."
He drove those cows away toward the teacher’s house;
for Yājñavalkya had claimed his own status as the most proficient in Brahman by accepting the wager regarding the one most learned in Brahman,
and at this the Brāhmaṇas became enraged.
He expresses their angry intent: "How can one among us, each of whom is preeminent, say, 'I am the most proficient in Brahman'?
Now, while the Brahmins were thus enraged, Janaka the sacrificer had a Hotṛ priest named Aśvala.
He [Aśvala] addressed Yājñavalkya:
Proud of his supreme Brahmanhood and emboldened by the king's patronage, he questioned Yājñavalkya.
How so? "Are you indeed, O Yājñavalkya, the most perfect knower of Brahman among us? (3)
The exclamation "pluti" is for the purpose of rebuking.
Yājñavalkya said: "We pay homage to the one most proficient in Brahman;
at present, we are desirous of cattle."

Since he was one who had pledged himself to the state of being most devoted to Brahman, it was precisely because of his acceptance of that wager regarding the most learned in Brahman that the Hotṛ Aśvala set his mind upon questioning him. //2//
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is overtaken by death, since all is seized by death, by what means does the sacrificer free himself from the reach of death?
"By the Hotṛ priest, by the fire, and by speech."
Speech, indeed, is the Hotṛ of the sacrifice.
Now, this speech is this very Agni; he is the Hotṛ; that is liberation; that is complete liberation.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said.

In that Madhu-kāṇḍa, the transcendence of death for the sacrificer through ritual action accompanied by the sevenfold meditation on the Udgītha was explained briefly in the section concerning the Udgītha.
This [present section] is begun as an elaboration for the sake of specific meditations pertaining to that very subject, as it is the domain of its further examination.

That is to say, this collection of means for this rite—such as the officiating priests, the fire, and so forth—is "attained" (*āpta*) by death characterized as action, accompanied by its inherent attachment;
it is not merely attained, but also "overwhelmed" (*abhibhūta*) and brought under the control of death.

By what means characterized as vision does the sacrificer overcome this attainment of death—that is, transcending the state of being subject to death—and become liberated, independent, and no longer subject to death? This is the meaning.
But has it not been stated in the section on the Udgītha that one is liberated by means of the vision of the Self as the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa)?
Certainly it was so stated;
however, there was a specific detail left unmentioned therein.
This undertaking is for that purpose; thus there is no fault.
Yājñavalkya says, "By the Hotṛ priest, by the fire, or by speech.
He explains the meaning of this as follows:
What, then, is the cause by which one transcends death?

It is said: Speech indeed belongs to the sacrificer of the sacrifice, according to the Vedic revelation, "The sacrifice is indeed the sacrificer. Of that sacrifice, of that sacrificer, whatever is speech, that is the Hotṛ priest with respect to the sacrifice.
How so? This triad is the body of the sacrifice and the sacrificer; this well-known Agni is the deity from the perspective of the higher gods (*adhidaivata*).
This has already been explained in the section concerning food.
And that Agni is the Hotṛ, according to the Vedic revelation: "Agni indeed is the Hotṛ."
This twofold means of accomplishing the sacrifice— the Hotṛ priest and the Adhvaryu priest with respect to the sacrifice,

and speech with respect to the self— this entire twofold means is "cut off," that is, seized by Death; it is brought under control by Death through action impelled by innate ignorance and attachment, undergoing a state of constant transformation at every moment.
Thus, by means of this Agni in his form as the presiding deity (adhidaivata), there occurs the liberation from the two paths of the sacrificer's sacrifice while it is yet unseen.
This is what he says: "He is liberation; He is the Hotṛ priest; Agni is liberation"—for the very perception of the true nature of Agni is itself liberation.
Precisely when the two means of accomplishment (sādhana) enter into the form of Agni,
at that very moment one is liberated from death consisting of natural attachment— from that which is internal and of limited form, as well as from that which is external and elemental.
Therefore, that Hotṛ priest, when perceived in the form of Agni, is liberation itself and the means of liberation for the sacrificer.
That is *atimukti*— whatever is liberation (*mukti*), that itself is *atimukti*, meaning it is the means for transcendent liberation (*atimukti*).
The vision of the two limited means of accomplishment as being of the nature of the unlimited presiding deity in the form of fire— that is liberation.

That which is liberation— the vision of the presiding deity (adhidevatā)— is itself called "transcendental liberation" (atimukti), which is the attainment of the state of the presiding deity, the state of fire, as the fruit resulting from having transcended death, which is the locus of attachment to the distinctions between the internal self (adhyātma) and the external elements (adhibhūta).
Considering that for this *atimukti* liberation itself is the means, he calls it *atimukti*.
For it has been explained in the section on the *Udgītha* that the *atimukti* of the sacrificer consists in the speech and other organs attaining the state of the fires and so forth.
In that context, it was stated that the mere perception of the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) in a general sense is the means to liberation.
That is not a distinction.
Here, the "seeing" of fire and so forth in speech and the other organs is described as the distinction;
however, liberation from death is that very state which constitutes the fruit.
This has been explained by the Udgītha Brāhmaṇa in the passage beginning with, "Having transcended death, he shines" (1.3.12). //3//
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is pervaded by day and night, and all is encompassed by day and night, by what means does the sacrificer transcend the pervasion of day and night?
"By the Adhvaryu priest, by the eye, and by the sun."
The Adhvaryu is indeed the eye of the sacrifice.
That which is this eye is yonder sun;
he is the Adhvaryu, that is liberation, that is complete liberation.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "the liberation from death characterized by action— which is prompted by innate ignorance and attachment— has been explained. Now,

regarding that death consisting of action along with its attachments, there is Time, which is the cause of the transformation of the means for performing rites such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices, which serve as the substratum for that death."

Because time is observed to function as the cause for the transformation of the means of action both before and after an action—even apart from its performance at a distinct time—liberation must be stated to be separate from that time. To this he says: "All this which is obtained through day and night;
and that time is of two forms: [the first] characterized by days and nights, etc."
And [it concerns] the characteristics of the lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth.

Among these, first, regarding the characteristics of the day and night (*ahorātra*) and so forth, he speaks of transcendence: "For by means of days and nights, everything is born, grows, and perishes; likewise, they are the means for accomplishing sacrifice."

The eye of the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu priest—these remaining syllables are to be understood as before. When the two means, the eye of the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu, having abandoned the limitations of the internal self (*adhyātma*) and the elemental world (*adhibhūta*), are perceived as the nature of the deities (*adhidaivata*), that is liberation; that Adhvaryu [is to be seen] in the form of the Sun.
"Seen is liberation.
That very liberation is indeed "supreme liberation.
As before, for one who has attained the nature of the sun, day and night do not exist. //4//

Now, liberation beyond the characteristics of the lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth is described: Yājñavalkya, he said, "Since all this is pervaded by the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*), and all is encompassed by the bright and dark fortnights— by what means does the sacrificer [cross over] the bright and dark fortnights?"
"By means of attainment he is released from transgression"—
that is, by means of the *udgātṛ* priest, by means of discernment, by means of breath.
For the *udgātṛ* is indeed the breath of the sacrifice.
Now, this vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed wind (vāyu); it is the Udgātṛ priest;
it is liberation (mukti), it is complete liberation (atimukti).

Now, liberation from the characteristics of lunar days and so forth is described: that which is this "all" [is governed by the sun]; the sun is the agent of day and night without distinction, but not of the lunar days such as the *pratipad* and others; for those, beginning with the *pratipad*, the moon is the agent through its undergoing of increase and decrease.
Therefore,
by the passing away of that [moon], there is the passing away of the bright and dark fortnights, just as there is the passing away of day and night by the passing away of the sun.
In this context, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the sacrificer is the wind (*vāyu*).
It is understood in the Udgītha Brāhmaṇa that he is indeed the Udgātṛ; this is determined by the statement, "For with speech and with breath he sang the Udgītha.
And it is also stated: "Now, water is the body of this breath, and its form of light is yonder moon.
Since there is identity between the breath, the wind, and the moon, there is no difference whether the conclusion is made with reference to the moon or the wind.
Thinking thus, the Śruti concludes by means of Vāyu in his form as the presiding deity (adhidaivata).
Moreover, since the waxing and waning of the moon are caused by Vāyu,
Vāyu is the agent of time— characterized by lunar days and so forth— and indeed its director.
Therefore, it is more logically consistent that one who has attained the form of air transcends time, such as the lunar days (tithis) and so forth.
Consequently, in another Vedic text (*śruti*), liberation (*mukti*) and transcendence of liberation (*atimukti*) are seen in the form of the moon;

whereas here, for the followers of the Kāṇva school, liberation and transcendence of liberation consist in viewing the two means [of knowledge] as having the nature of air, which is their cause. Thus, there is no contradiction between the two Vedic texts. //5//
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "by what means does the sacrificer ascend to the heavenly world from this atmosphere which is, as it were, without support?
By the Brahman priest, by the mind, and by the moon."
The mind, indeed, is the Brahman-priest of the sacrifice.
That which is this mind is yonder moon; he is the Brahman, he is liberation, he is complete liberation—these are the means of transcendence.
Now follow the correspondences.

The liberation of the sacrificer from death—that is, from time—has been explained. Now it is stated by what support that person, being liberated, transcends death which consists of limitation and attains the fruit; thus he is said to be "liberated.

This well-known intermediate space, the ether (*ākāśa*), is "without support" (*anārambaṇa*)—the word "as if" (*iva*) implies that there certainly is a support there, but its nature is not known; this is the intended meaning.
That which is the unknown objective support (ālambana) is asked about by means of the pronoun "what" (kena);
otherwise, the attainment of the fruit would be impossible.
The subject of the question is: "What is that by means of which the sacrificer, supported [by it], attains the fruit of the action and is thereby liberated without delay?"

By what sequence does the sacrificer ascend to the heavenly world? The meaning is that he attains the heavenly world as his fruit; he is "liberated" (atimucyate). The arrangement of the syllables—*brahmaṇā ṛtvijā manasā candreṇa*—is as before.
Therein, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*), that which is well-known as the mind of the sacrificer in the sacrifice is the moon (*candra*) with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*).
It is well known that the mind is the internal [correspondence] and the moon is the divine correspondence (*adhidevatam*).

That very moon, through the priestly function of Brahman, is the limited form pertaining to the elements (*adhibhūtam*), while the Brāhmaṇa is the limited form pertaining to the internal mind. One perceives this dyad through the unlimited form of the moon;
by means of that moon as the support for the mind, one attains the world of heaven, the fruit of action, and is thereby liberated—this is the intended meaning.
The word "iti" (thus) is for the purpose of conclusion.
These are the various modes of liberation from death (*atimokṣa*).
Since all the modes of vision (*darśana*) concerning the components of sacrifice (*yajñāṅga*) have been stated on this occasion, they are summarized as "liberations" (*atimokṣāḥ*).
This means that such are the types of liberation.
Now, as for the perfections:
next, the perfections are now being explained.

"Accomplishment" (*sampat*) refers to the bringing about of the results of great, fruitful rites such as the *agnihotra* and others by means of some commonality; or it is the impossibility [of achieving the result] due to some deficiency for those who, with all their energy, strive to perform the means of attaining the result. Now, one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), having taken up any rite whatsoever—such as the *agnihotra*—as possible according to its nature and made it his object of focus, while possessing knowledge of the fruits of action, whatever fruit of action he desires, that very [fruit]...

He accomplishes it; otherwise, even for those of the three higher castes who are entitled to perform the Rājasūya, Aśvamedha, Puruṣamedha, and Sarvamedha sacrifices, their recitation of those texts would be merely for the sake of private study (svādhyāya),
provided there were no means whatsoever for attaining their fruits.

Therefore, for them, the attainment of that fruit occurs through the very act of identification; thus, even identifications possess fruitfulness. Consequently, the identifications are now commenced. //6//
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "with how many ṛg-verses will this Hotṛ priest perform today at this sacrifice? "With three," he replied.
"What are those three?
"The *puronuvākyā*, the *yājyā*, and the *śasyā* as the third.
"What does one win by means of them?"
"Whatever there is here that possesses breath. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.7)
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, in order to draw his attention:

"With how many Ṛks will this Hotṛ priest perform his recitation (śastra) today at this sacrifice? With how many—that is, with what number—of Ṛks, or types of Ṛks, will he recite? The other replied: "With three types of Ṛks."
To him who had spoken thus, the other replied: "Which are those three?
This question concerns the object to be enumerated (*saṅkhyeya*), whereas the previous one concerned the number itself (*saṅkhyā*).
The verses that are employed prior to the conclusion of the sacrifice are called *puronuvākyā*, which is a class of *ṛc* verses;
those *ṛc* verses that are employed for the purpose of the sacrifice [are called *yajyā*].
That class of *ṛc* which serves as the *yājyā* is the *ṛgjāti* used for the purpose of the *śastra*; those *ṛcs* which are employed for the *śastra* are that *ṛgjāti* used as the *śasya*.
Whatever ṛcs there may be—whether they are stotriyas or others—all of them are included within these three types of ṛcs.
What does one win by means of them? "Whatever here is endowed with breath"—therefore, because of this similarity in number, whatever is born as a living being, [is won].
It conquers all that and accomplishes the entire range of results through its commonality with number and other such qualities. //7//
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many oblations will the Adhvaryu offer today in this sacrifice? "Three," he replied.
"What are those three? "Those which, when offered, blaze up; those which, when offered, overflow; and those which, when offered, lie still.
"What does one win by means of them?"
Those oblations which, when offered, blaze up, by them he conquers the world of the gods;
for the world of the gods, as it were, blazes forth.
Those oblations which, when offered, go out, by them he conquers the world of the fathers.
For the world of the fathers is, as it were, high up;
by those [oblations] which, once offered, remain on the fire, he conquers the world of men,
for the world of men is, as it were, below.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, as before.
"How many kinds of oblations will this Adhvaryu priest offer in this sacrifice today?"— that is, how many varieties of oblations are there?

Regarding the phrase "those three": "Which are those three? is as explained previously. The other replied: "Those oblations of fuel-sticks and clarified butter which, when offered, blaze up; those oblations of meat and so forth which, when offered, overflow—that is, produce an excessive sound;
and those oblations of milk and soma which, when offered, lie down—that is, having gone beneath the fire, they lie upon the earth."
"What does he conquer by means of those?"—
that is, what does he conquer by means of those oblations thus produced?
Those oblations which, when offered, blaze— that is, those oblations which are produced as being endowed with blazing.
And the fruit known as the world of the gods is indeed radiant;

by means of that common quality, he effects this identification: "These oblations being prepared, which are themselves radiant, are the very form of the world of the gods—the fruit of action—and thus it is the fruit called the world of the gods itself that is being prepared by me.
In this way, he brings about the correspondence.
Those oblations which, when offered, transcend [the world], by means of them one conquers the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka), due to the commonality of being the producers of contemptible sounds.
One conquers the world of the ancestors by means of them because of that commonality of producing contemptible sounds;
for in the city of Saṃyamanī, which is connected to the world of the ancestors, as those being led away by Vaivasvata, there arises the sound: "Alas! We are slain! Release us! Release us!"

Likewise, by means of the oblations of *avadāna* (cuttings), he accomplishes the thought: "Since this is common to the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*), it is the world of the ancestors itself that I am producing.
Those oblations which remain after being offered conquer the world of men alone, because of the commonality of their connection with the surface of the earth;
for the world of men is, as it were, below—lower indeed—when compared to the higher worlds of the *sādhya*s.
Alternatively, with reference to downward movement,
he accomplishes [his aim] by thinking, "I shall bring about [the result] right here in the world of humans.
Those oblations which are placed upon the fire conquer the world of humans alone, because of the common connection with the earth above.
For the world of men is indeed "below," in relation to the higher worlds of the Sādhyas, or in relation to the downward movement [of the moon].
Therefore, at the time of performing the oblations of milk and Soma, he brings it about, thinking, "The world of men itself is being produced by me. //8//
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "with how many deities does this Brahman protect the sacrifice today from the south? "With one," he replied.
"What is that one? "It is the mind alone. "The mind is indeed infinite; the All-Gods are infinite."
By that very [truth], he conquers the infinite world.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, as before.
This priest, the Brahman, standing on the south at the Brahman's seat, protects the sacrifice.
"By how many deities does he protect it?"—this plural number is used here incidentally.
For he protects by means of a single deity;

when this is known, a question in the plural number is not appropriate for one who knows it himself. Therefore, having observed the pattern in the questions and answers of the two preceding sections—where "by how many? is answered with "by three," and "how many? with "three"—here too [the plural] is used.
The introduction to the question is now undertaken;
or alternatively, the plural number is used for the purpose of confusing the opponent.
The other says: "By one"—that is, by that single deity by whom, standing to the south, the sacrifice is protected at the seat of Brahman.
"What is she who possesses the *sai*?
"It is the mind itself. The mind is that deity; for Brahmā exerts himself through the mind alone by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
“Of that sacrifice, mind and speech are the two paths; the Brahman priest prepares one of them by means of the mind,” according to another scriptural passage (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.16.1).
Therefore, the mind itself is the deity, for by means of that mind the Brahman priest protects the sacrifice.
And that mind is infinite due to the diversity of its modifications (*vṛtti*).
The word "vai" is for the purpose of indicating what is well-known;
the infinity of the mind is well-known.
Then there are the gods who possess the conceit of infinity, based on another scriptural passage stating, "wherein all the gods become one," and so forth.
Because of that commonality of infinity, he indeed conquers that world which is infinite. //9//
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many *stotriya* hymns will this Udgātṛ chant today at this sacrifice? "Three," he replied.
Which are those three?
The *puronuvākyā*, the *yājyā*, and the *śasyā* as the third.
Which are they?
Regarding the phrase "that which is internal":
the out-breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the *puronuvākyā*, the in-breath (*apāna*) is the *yājyā*, and the diffused breath (*vyāna*) is the *śasyā*.
What does one win by means of these?
"By the invitatory verse (puronuvākyā) one conquers the world of earth; by the offering verse (yājyā), the world of the intermediate space; and by the recitation verse (śasyā), the world of heaven.
Thereupon, Aśvala, the Hotṛ priest, ceased questioning.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, as before. "How many *stotriyas* will the Udgātṛ chant?
A *stotriya* is a collection of several verses (*ṛk*) belonging to a *sāman*.
Regarding the verses for the *stotriya*, the *anuvāśamyā*, and so forth—whatever these verses may be—he says that they are all three in number.
And these have been explained: "The invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), the offering verse (*yājyā*), and the recitation (*śasyā*) as the third."

In this regard, it was previously stated: "Whatever there is here that possesses breath, he conquers all of that. By what commonality is this so? It is said: "Which are those three *ṛc*s that exist with respect to the self (*adhyātma*)? The vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself is the *puronuvākyā*.
Because of the commonality of the word *paśu*,
the *yājyā* belongs to the *avāna*, due to its immediate sequence.
For the deities swallow the oblation offered by the *apāna*;
and sacrifice is an offering.
Regarding the *vyāna*, it is said: “Without breathing out and without breathing in, he utters the *ṛc*” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.4).
Thus, from another scriptural source (*śrutyantara*).
It has been explained what one conquers by means of those [vows].
In that context, the general connection with the specific [details] was not stated; it is stated here.
Everything else has been explained.
By means of the commonality of connection with the world, one conquers the world of earth through the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*),
and the world of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) through the offering verse (*yājyā*).
Because of the commonality of being in the middle;
and because of the commonality of being upward with respect to the portion of the heavenly world.
Then, from that resolution of the questions regarding the Self, that Hotṛ Aśvala desisted, thinking, "He is not within our reach. //10//
Thus ends the first Aśvala-Brāhmaṇa in the third chapter. //1//
The connection with the narrative is well known.
Liberation from death—characterized by time and characterized by action—has been explained.
But who is this death from which liberation has been explained?

And that death consists of the seat of innate ignorance and attachment, delimited by the internal self (adhyātma), the elements (adhibhūta), and their objects; it is characterized by the organs of perception (graha) and their objects (atigraha).
Therefore, the forms of him who is liberated from that death which is of a delimited nature—the forms such as fire, the sun, and so forth—have been explained in the section on the Udgītha.
In the Aśvala-Prasna, there is a certain specific detail regarding that same subject.
And this is the fruit of actions when accompanied by knowledge.
Since liberation must be achieved from this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) consisting of the nature of the goal and the means, the true nature of death—which is of the form of bondage—is now described;
for liberation can only be effected for one who is bound.
Even regarding that which was described as the nature of one who has transcended, there too he is indeed not liberated from death in the form of the *graha* (seizing) and *atigraha* (over-seizing).
Thus it has been said: "Hunger is death" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.1), and "This very thing is death."
Referring to the Person dwelling in the sun, he says, "Death is one, [but for others] it is many.
For it is said that one who has attained the state of being that Self is liberated from death;
yet in that state, the graspers (*graha*) and over-graspers (*atigraha*), which are forms of death, have not ceased to exist.
"Furthermore, of this mind, heaven is the body, and its form of light is yonder sun" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.12);
"And the mind is a grasper; it is seized by desire as the over-grasper" (3.2.7);
and he will further state: "Prāṇa indeed is a grasper; it is seized by apāna as the over-grasper" (3.2.2).
2) Thus [it is said], "Speech indeed is the grāha; it is surpassed by the name as the atigrāha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.2.3).
This has been explained by us in the section on the division of food.
And this has been well-considered: that which is the cause of engagement is not itself the cause of cessation.
Some, however, consider everything to be a cause of cessation.

For this reason, as one is released from each preceding death and attains each succeeding one, one attains them solely for the purpose of turning away [from the former], and not for the sake of that [attainment] itself;
therefore, until the destruction of duality, everything is death.
But upon the cessation of duality, one attains the ultimate reality and is completely liberated from death;
therefore, liberation in the intermediate state is merely relative and secondary.
All of this is indeed according to the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

[Objection: Is it not the case that liberation is the oneness of all, according to the Vedic scripture: "Therefore, it became all this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10)? [Reply: Certainly, this is also so; however, [it does not contradict] such injunctions as, "One who desires a village should sacrifice," and so forth.
The purpose of scriptural passages such as "One desiring cattle should sacrifice" is for that [very end].
For if these [passages] had non-duality as their sole meaning, then ends such as villages, cattle, and heaven would not exist; yet, the various specific fruits of ritual action are indeed perceived.
And if Vedic rituals were solely for that purpose [of liberation], then transmigratory existence itself would not have come to be.
If it is argued that even while being for that purpose, transmigratory existence is of the nature of a by-product (*anuniṣpādita-padārtha-svabhāva*), [we reply:]...
And just as, for the purpose of seeing forms, everything situated there is indeed illuminated by light;
[this is not so], because no proof is established.
Regarding the non-dual meaning of Vedic rituals when accompanied by knowledge (*vidyā*), there is no proof established for their being produced as something else.
Therefore, it is neither perception nor inference, and for that very reason, it is not scripture either.
If it is argued that both [perception and inference] are demonstrated by a single sentence— just as in the cases of the channeling of a stream or the illumination of light—
that is not so, because the properties of a sentence do not apply [to such things].
Furthermore, it is not possible to understand that the meaning contained within a single sentence serves as a means for either engagement or desisting from action;
there is no fault in this because, in cases such as the leading of irrigation channels or the lighting of lamps, the purpose is directly perceptible.
As for what is also said—that mantras are observed to have this [practical] purpose—[that too is incorrect].
This very point, however, is accessible through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
As for the mantras, it remains to be investigated whether they pertain to this matter or to some other matter.
Therefore, death, characterized by the seizing and over-seizing [of the senses], is bondage.

Therefore, since it must be stated what is to be enjoyed, this [section] begins: "And we do not consider it a clever stratagem—like the 'half-old woman' (ardha-jarati) parable—to posit a state of existence in the interval between the objects of experience.
As for the fact that after saying "one is liberated from death," the "seizers" (graha) and "over-seizers" (atigraha) are mentioned, that is because of their connection to the subject matter.
All this bondage, characterized by the means and the goal of attainment, arises from the failure to release oneself from the grasp and the over-grasp;
for indeed, once the shackles are fully understood, an effort must be made for the liberation of the one bound.
Therefore, this [inquiry] is undertaken for that purpose.
Now, Jāratkārava Ārtabhāga questioned him.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many are the *grahas* (seizers) and how many are the *atigrahas* (over-seizers)?
"There are eight *grahas* and eight *atigrahas*.
"Which are those eight *grahas* and eight *atigrahas*? 3.2.1.
Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 3.2.1: Now, the particle *ha* indicates tradition (*aitihya*).

Immediately thereafter, when Aśvala had ceased speaking, Ārtabhāga—born of the Jaratkāru lineage, thus called Jāratkārava, and being the offspring of Ṛtabhāga—questioned Yājñavalkya, who was the subject under discussion. He addressed him, saying, "O Yājñavalkya," as before, in order to draw his attention, and asked: "How many *grahas* (seizers) are there, and how many *atigrahas* (over-seizers)?"
The word *iti* serves to mark the conclusion of the sentence.
In that regard, the question would arise either when the *grahas* (seizers) and *atigrahas* (over-seizers) are already known, or when they are not yet known.

If the *grahas* and *atigrahas* were already known, then since their quality—namely, their number—would also be known, a question concerning their number, such as "How many *grahas* are there? How many *atigrahas* are there?", would be inappropriate.

If, on the other hand, they were not already known, then the question would concern their number as its object; one would have to ask, "Which are the *grahas* and which are the *atigrahas*," rather than asking, "How many *grahas* are there and how many *atigrahas*?
Furthermore, a question regarding specific details arises only when the general category is already known, such as, "Which among these are the Kaṭhas? Which among these are the Kālāpas?
Moreover, no entities named *grahas* and *atigrahas* are well-known in the world.
By this, there would be a question regarding a specific meaning.

But has it not already been stated that "he is liberated"? For liberation belongs to one who was seized by a grasper; thus it has been stated twice: "that is liberation, that is transcendental liberation" (*atimukti*).
Therefore, both the graspers (*graha*) and the over-graspers (*atigraha*) are established.

[Objection: But even there, the four *grahas* and *atigrahas*—namely speech, sight, breath, and mind—are already known; therefore, the question "how many? is not appropriate because they have been ascertained. [Reply: No, because it is for the sake of non-determination.

For the number four was not intended to be emphasized there, but here, since the *grahas* and *atigrahas* are being presented, the question "how many? is indeed appropriate, as it intends to emphasize the quality of their being eight.
Therefore, since "mukti" and "atimukti" are stated twice as "mukti" and "atimukti," the "grahas" and "atigrahas" are also established by implication.
Consequently, he asks: "How many are the grahas, and how many are the atigrahas?
The other replies: "There are eight grahas and eight atigrahas."
Regarding those eight planets that have been mentioned, which among them are to be seized according to the rule? //1//
The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the grasper; it is seized by the out-breath (apāna) as the over-grasper.
For by means of the vital breath one smells odors.
Regarding this, the text says:
"The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the grasper. Here, "vital breath" refers to the sense of smell, because of the context.
That [nose] is accompanied by air; "by the out-breath" (apāna) means "by the odor" (gandha). Because it is associated with the out-breath, the out-breath is called "odor."
For indeed, every person in the world smells an odor brought forth by the *apāna* [vital air] with the sense of smell; therefore, it is said: "By means of the *apāna*, one smells odors. //2//
Speech, indeed, is the grasper;
it is seized by the name as the over-grasper.
For it is by speech that one utters names.
The tongue, indeed, is a grasper;
it is seized by taste as the over-grasper, for by means of the tongue one perceives tastes. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.4)
The eye, indeed, is the grasper; it is seized by form as the over-grasper, for one sees forms with the eye. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.5)
The ear, indeed, is the grasper;
it is seized by sound as the over-grasper,
for by means of the ear one hears sounds.
The mind, indeed, is a grasper; it is seized by desire as the over-grasper,
for by means of the mind one desires desires.
The hands, indeed, are the grasper;
they are seized by action as the over-grasper,
for it is with the hands that one performs action.
The skin, indeed, is a grasper;
it is seized by touch as the over-grasper,
for by means of the skin one perceives touches.
Thus there are eight graspers and eight over-graspers.
Speech indeed is the grasper (*graha*).

For by speech—which, when limited to the internal self, has as its domain objects of attachment, and which is occupied with speaking what is untrue, false, indecent, and loathsome—the world is seized and carried away by it; thus speech is the grasper. That [speech] is seized by the over-grasper (*atigraha*), namely Name (*nāman*); that grasper called speech is [seized] by Name, the object to be spoken, which is the over-grasper.

Regarding the term *atigrāheṇa*, the lengthening [of the vowel] is a Vedic (Chāndasa) usage. "Speech" (*vāk*) refers to that which is to be spoken; for speech is employed for the sake of the object to be expressed—that is, it is directed toward that purpose—and is thus brought under control by that object. Therefore, unless it performs its function, there is no liberation for it.
Hence, speech is said to be "seized" by the name as its *atigrāha*.
For one who engages with speech through attachment is joined with all manner of misfortunes;
the rest is the same.
Thus, these eight beginning with the skin are the "grasps" (graha), and these eight ending with touch are the "over-grasps" (atigraha). // 3.9 //
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is food for death, who is that deity for whom death is food?
"Fire, indeed, is death; it is the food of water."
Moreover, he conquers repeated death.

When the *grahas* and *atigrahas* had been withdrawn, he spoke again: "O Yājñavalkya," he said, "this entire world is food for Death; indeed, everything that is differentiated is food for Death, for everything is born and perishes, being swallowed by Death in the form of the *grahas* and *atigrahas*.
Who then might be that deity for whom even Death would be food?"
"Death is the condiment for it," according to another Vedic text.
This is the intention of the questioner:
if he were to speak of a death of death, there would be an infinite regress.
If he does not speak, then liberation from this death characterized by the graspers (*graha*) and the over-graspers (*atigraha*) would not be possible;
for liberation occurs only upon the destruction of death consisting of the graspers and over-graspers.

If there were even a death of death itself, then the destruction of death characterized by the graspers and over-graspers would be possible. Therefore, considering the question difficult to answer, he asks: "Which indeed is that deity?"
There is, indeed, a death of death. But would this not lead to an infinite regress, since there would be yet another death for that one as well?
No, there is no infinite regress.
Because no death can occur within death itself.
But how is it known that there is a death of death?
Because it is observed.
Fire, for its part, is seen as the death of everything because it causes destruction;
that fire is consumed by water, and that fire is the food of water.
Therefore, accept this: there exists a death even of death.
By that [knowledge], everything born of the *grahas* and *atigrahas* is devoured by the death of death.
When that bondage has been destroyed and devoured by death, liberation from *saṃsāra* becomes possible.
For it has been stated that bondage is characterized by the *grahas* and *atigrahas*, and it has thus been established that liberation arises from that.
Therefore, human effort for the sake of bondage and liberation becomes fruitful; thus, one overcomes death once again. //10//
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, do his vital breaths depart from him, or not? "No," said Yājñavalkya.
Right here they are completely dissolved;
it swells up and becomes distended.
Swollen, he lies dead.

When this person— the liberated knower who has been freed by the vision of the Supreme Self after Death has been swallowed by the Higher Death— dies at whatever time, do the vital breaths (prāṇas), such as speech and the rest, which are the "graspers" (grahas), and the "over-graspers" (atigrahas), which are the latent impressions (vāsanās) residing within and acting as motivators, depart upwards from this dying knower of Brahman, or do they not?
"No," said Yājñavalkya, "they do not depart; rather, right here in this very person, they attain non-distinction with the supreme Self.

The effects and the instruments [of the senses] are merged—that is, they are dissolved into a state of oneness—in their own source, which is the true essence of the Supreme Brahman, within the Knower."

Like waves in the ocean; and likewise, another scriptural passage shows the dissolution of the vital breaths, which are denoted by the word "parts" (kalā), into the supreme Self: "In this very way, these sixteen parts of this all-seeing one, which have the Puruṣa as their goal, reach the Puruṣa and go to their setting."
Thus it is shown that they go to non-distinction with the supreme Self.
In that case, is he not dead?
No, indeed.
And because this [body] is dead, it swells—that is, it attains a state of inflation—and distends, being filled with external air like a bellows;
thus, the dead one lies motionless, inflated like a leather bag. The meaning of the sentence is that, upon the destruction of its bonds, there is no going anywhere for the liberated one. //11//
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, what does not leave him?"
"Name"—name is indeed infinite, and the All-gods are infinite; he wins an infinite world by means of that. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.12.
Regarding the liberated one: do only the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) merge away, or does everything that causes them also merge?
Or is it that only the vital breaths merge while their cause remains;
for if the cause were present, there would be the recurrence of the vital breaths?
Now, since liberation is possible only if everything— including desire, action, and so forth— is [abandoned], for this purpose the following question was asked:
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, what does not leave him?"
"Everything is merged into what is called the 'other than name' (nāmaitara)" means that everything is dissolved;
however, the mere name itself is not dissolved because of its connection with the form (ākṛti),
for the name is eternal.
"Ananta" indeed means "endless. Endlessness is the very nature of the name.
The Viśvedevas, who are presided over by that endlessness, are themselves endless; through that [name], he conquers an endless world.
Having approached all the gods presiding over that infinity as one's own self, one conquers the infinite world itself by means of that vision of infinity. //12//

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person has died, into what does his speech merge? Into the fire, his breath; into the wind, his sight; into the sun, his mind; into the moon, his hearing; into the quarters, his body; into space, his self (ātman); into the plants, his body hairs; and into the trees, his hair of the head?"
"The hair, blood, and semen are deposited in the waters; where then does this person come to be? "Come, my dear Ārtabhāga, let us two alone know this; this is not for us to discuss in public."
Having stepped out, the two of them deliberated.
Whatever they said, they spoke of nothing but action;
and whatever they praised, they praised nothing but action.
"One becomes virtuous by virtuous action and evil by evil action.
Thereupon, Ārtabhāga Jāratkārava fell silent.

The bondage consisting of the *grahas* (senses) and *atigrahas* (objects), which is of the nature of death, has been described; and since there exists a death of that death, liberation is also possible.
That liberation consists in the dissolution right here of the *grahas* and *atigrahas*, like the extinguishing of a lamp.
Just as this bondage called *graha* and *atigraha* is of the nature of death, this [section] is now commenced in order to determine the true nature of that which causes it.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said.
Regarding this, some explain as follows: even when the "graspers" (grahas) and "over-graspers" (atigrahas), along with their causal agents, have been destroyed, one is indeed not yet liberated.

Remaining only as a name, like a saline wasteland produced from one's own self, the self remains delimited from itself and separated from the world of objects to be enjoyed, persisting in the interval between the cessation of desire and action.

Since the perception of duality must be removed by means of the vision of the oneness of the Supreme Self (paramātman), they establish a connection with the subsequent text by postulating an intermediate state called liberation (apavarga), asserting that the vision of the Supreme Self must now be commenced.

To this, it must be asked: how can there be hearing, reflection, and meditative contemplation (śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana) upon the vision of the Supreme Self for one who is bodiless and whose sense organs have dissolved?
For they say that one whose vital breaths have been withdrawn and who remains as a mere name is "lying dead";
this cannot be established even by way of a mere mental conceit.

Now, if it is postulated that while still alive, one remains with only ignorance remaining and has turned away from the object of enjoyment (*bhojya*), then it must be stated what the cause of that is.
If it is argued that the cause is the attainment of the Self as the unity of all duality, that has already been refuted.

[For] the knower, endowed with the vision of the Self as the unity of duality accompanied by ritual action, upon death and the dissolution of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), [attains] the state of being the Self of the universe.

Or, one whose vital breaths have not yet been merged [into the elements] might attain the very nature of Hiraṇyagarbha; yet, being detached from what is to be enjoyed even while living, he would become oriented toward the vision of the Supreme Self.
And these two goals cannot be obtained through a single means accomplished by a single effort.
If it is a means for attaining Hiraṇyagarbha, it is not a means for turning away from him;
and if it is a means for turning away from the objects of enjoyment in order to bring about orientation toward the Supreme Self, it is not a means for attaining Hiraṇyagarbha.
For that which is a means for reaching a certain state cannot also be a means for the cessation of reaching that same state.
Then, having died and attained Hiraṇyagarbha, one whose vital breaths have been withdrawn and who remains as nothing but name becomes qualified for the knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Consequently, the instruction of the knowledge of the Supreme Self for the sake of those such as ourselves would be purposeless;
for it is by means of such scriptural passages as "Whosoever among the gods... that the knowledge of Brahman is taught for the fulfillment of the human goal for all.
Therefore, this conception is utterly base and entirely outside the scope of the scriptures.
We shall, however, proceed with the subject at hand.
With the desire to determine by what this bondage, characterized by the *grahas* (seizers) and *atigrahas* (over-seizers), is impelled, [the text] says: "In which..."

For a person who has not attained right vision—who possesses a head, hands, and so forth—when he dies, speech goes into fire, breath goes into wind, and sight goes into the sun; this [verb] "goes into" is to be connected with every instance.
"Mind into the moon, the quarters into hearing, the body into the earth, and the self (ātman) into space"—here, by "self," the space within the heart, which is the locus of the self, is meant.
He enters into space; his body hairs enter into the plants;
his head hairs enter into the trees.
"The blood and the semen are deposited in the waters"—this is an indicative mark of their being taken up again.

For everywhere, by words such as "speech" and so forth, the deities are intended, and not merely the instruments themselves depart prior to liberation. In that state, when the instruments are no longer presided over by the deities and are comparable to discarded tools like a sickle, it is asked—what does the bodiless agent, the person, who has become independent, rest upon? "Where is he then? [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13]
"It becomes a person.
[The question is: "Depending on what does it then become a person?

This is the inquiry: "What is that substratum, depending upon which it again takes up the aggregate of effects and instruments, by means of which the bondage characterized by the 'grasps' (graha) and 'over-grasps' (atigraha) is applied?"

To this it is replied: Proponents have postulated [theories] such as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), chance (*yadṛcchā*), time (*kāla*), karma, destiny (*daiva*), mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*), and emptiness (*śūnya*).
Because there are thus many points of disagreement, the determination of the reality cannot be reached through the method of debate (*jalpanyāya*).
If you desire the determination of the reality here, come, O Somya, let us two—Sārtabhāga and I—investigate and determine that which is to be known regarding what you have asked.
Why?
Because this matter cannot be decided between us in the presence of people, amidst a crowd of men;
therefore, we shall go to a secluded place for deliberation.
"Those two," and so forth, is the statement of the Śruti.
It is now told what those two—Yājñavalkya and Ārtabhāga—did after going to a secluded place: "Having gone out from that place where people were, they deliberated.
At first, they examined each of the positions of worldly disputants one by one.

Listen to what those two said after deliberating and setting aside all prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣas*): they both declared that action (*karman*) alone is the basis, the cause for the repeated assumption of the body and the organs. Not only among the accepted causes such as time, action, destiny, and God did they praise it, but they praised action alone.

Since it has been determined that this appropriation of the instruments and effects, such as the *grahas* and *atigrahas*, is repeatedly impelled by karma, therefore one indeed becomes meritorious through meritorious action prescribed by the scriptures, and conversely, one becomes its opposite— sinful— through sinful action.
When Yājñavalkya had thus reached a definitive conclusion in his answers, Jaratkārava, because Yājñavalkya was unshakable, [ceased].
Ārtabhāga fell silent. //13//
Thus ends the second Ārtabhāga Brāhmaṇa in the third chapter.
Then Bhujyu Lāhyāyani questioned him. "O Yājñavalkya," he said, "we were wandering as students among the Madras.
We came to the house of Patañcala Kāpya."
He had a daughter who was possessed by a Gandharva.
We asked him, "Who are you?
and he replied, "I am Sudhanvan Āṅgirasa."
When we asked him about the ends of the worlds, he said this to us: "Where did the Pārikṣitas go?
Where did the Pārikṣitas go?"
I ask you that, Yājñavalkya:
where did the Pārikṣitas go?
Now, Bhujyu Lāhyāyani questioned him:
"The bondage characterized by the *grahas* (seizers) and *atigrahas* (over-seizers) has been described.
That from which one is released when freed—along with its cause—or that by which one is bound and wanders in transmigratory existence, is Death."
And from that, liberation is possible;
because for one who dies there is further death,
whereas for one who is liberated there is no going anywhere.
It has been determined that total destruction leaves nothing but a mere name, like the extinguishing of a lamp.

In this regard, for those wandering in saṃsāra and those being liberated, the dissolution of their effects and instruments into their own causes is the same; yet, while for the liberated there is an absolute non-reappropriation [of causes], for those wandering in saṃsāra there is repeated reappropriation. That by which they are impelled is determined, following thorough investigation, to be karma.
And upon the destruction of that [karma], when nothing but the name remains, liberation is the cessation of everything.
And that consists of the karma known as merit and demerit,
because it has been established that "one becomes virtuous through virtuous action and sinful through sinful action."

This world-process is brought about by that [karman]. Therein, through demerit (apuṇya), one experiences suffering among stationary and moving beings—which abound in natural misery—as well as in the hells, among animals, and among the hungry ghosts (preta), being born and dying again and again; this is as well-known to all the world as the royal highway.
However, regarding that which is scriptural—namely, "One indeed becomes meritorious through meritorious action"—it is toward this that the Veda here bestows its emphasis.
All the declarations of the Śruti and Smṛti maintain that meritorious action alone is the means for accomplishing all human goals (puruṣārtha).
Since liberation (mokṣa) is also a human goal, it follows that it must be achievable through such means.
To the extent that there is an excellence of merit, to that same extent is the attainment of excellence in the fruit.
Therefore, the doubt might arise that liberation will result from the excellence of merit alone;
this must be dispelled [by the teaching that] such is the ultimate reach of even the most distinguished action when accompanied by knowledge,
because both action and its fruit have as their locus name-and-form (nāmarūpa) which has been manifested.
However, there is no operation of karma in that which is non-action, eternal, characterized as unmanifest (avyākṛta), devoid of name and form, and stripped of the nature of action, agent, and fruit;
and since wherever there is such an operation, that is indeed saṃsāra, it is for the purpose of demonstrating this point that the inquiry into Brahman is commenced.

As for what some say—that karma accompanied by knowledge, when performed without desire for results, initiates a different effect, just as poison mixed with mantras or curd mixed with sugar does—[that is not so].
That is not so,
because liberation is not something to be undertaken;
for liberation is simply the destruction of bondage and is not an effect to be produced, and we have already stated that bondage is ignorance.
Furthermore, the destruction of ignorance through karma is not tenable,
because the efficacy of karma has a perceptible domain;
for the objects of the efficacy of karma are indeed origination, acquisition, modification, and refinement.
The capacity of karma consists in producing, attaining, and transforming; therefore, there is no object for the power of karma other than these.
This is because such a thing is not established in the world, and liberation (mokṣa) is not any one of these categories of things.
We have stated that [the Self] is separated by ignorance alone.
Very well;
let it be that action alone has such a nature.
But for one who is endowed with knowledge and free from intentional desire, the nature [of action] becomes otherwise.
For it is observed that even substances such as poison or curd, whose powers are well known, possess a different capacity when combined with spells, mantras, sugar, and so forth;
let it be the same for action as well—if this is argued, we say no.
Because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For in that case, regarding the existence of a capacity for action toward an object other than those already mentioned, there is no valid means of knowledge—neither perception, nor inference, nor analogy, nor presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), nor verbal testimony.
[Objection: But surely, in the absence of any other result, the fact that the injunction (*codanā*) would otherwise be inexplicable is the valid means of knowledge.
For in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*), a fruit is not postulated according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice,
nor is there any scripturally stated fruit;
yet they are nevertheless enjoined.
By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is understood that liberation is their fruit;
otherwise, persons would not engage [in the practice].
But is it not the case that the very logic of the Viśvajit sacrifice applies here, since liberation is postulated as the fruit?

If no fruit—whether liberation or something else—were postulated, persons would not engage in [the practice]; therefore, liberation is postulated as the fruit through the presumption based on the scriptural meaning (*śrutārthāpatti*), just as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice.
But if this is so, how can it be said that the principle of the Viśvajit does not apply?
To say that "a fruit is postulated" and yet "the principle of the Viśvajit does not apply" is a contradictory statement.
If it is argued that liberation (*mokṣa*) is not indeed a fruit, we say no; for that would entail the abandonment of your own thesis.
For you have already asserted that karma initiates another effect, just like poison mixed with curd and so forth.
If liberation is not the very fruit that is the effect of action, then that proposition would be abandoned.
Furthermore, if liberation were the effect of action, one must state the distinction between it and fruits such as heaven.
Alternatively, if it is not the effect of action, then you must explain the meaning of this formulation: "Liberation is the fruit of obligatory (nitya) actions."
Nor can a distinction be postulated merely on the basis of a difference in terminology regarding "effect" and "fruit.

For it would be contradictory to assert that liberation—which is not a fruit—is produced by eternal rites, and that the fruit of eternal rites is not an effect; this is like saying "fire is cold," or like claiming it is "like knowledge. If you say [this is not so] because [knowledge] is like fire... [the argument continues].

If it is argued that just as liberation is said to be the effect of knowledge—even though it is not produced by knowledge—likewise [liberation] may be said to have action as its effect; we say no. Because knowledge functions to remove ignorance, liberation is figuratively called the effect of knowledge, since knowledge removes the obstruction of ignorance.
But ignorance is not to be removed by action;
nor can any other obstacle to liberation be postulated apart from ignorance,
because liberation is eternal and non-different from the very nature of the seeker.
If it is argued that karma might turn back ignorance, we say no,
because their natures are dissimilar.
Non-manifestation is ignorance (*ajñāna*), and it is opposed by knowledge (*jñāna*) characterized by manifestation.
Action (*karman*), however, is opposed by that [ignorance]; therefore, action is distinct from knowledge.
Whether ignorance is said to be the absence of knowledge, doubt, or erroneous knowledge, all of it is indeed sublated by knowledge alone.
But it is not [removed] by any other action, because there is no contradiction [between knowledge and action].

If it is argued that the unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*) of actions must be postulated as the remover of ignorance, we say no; for when the removal of ignorance through knowledge is already established, the postulation of the removal of an unseen potency is untenable.

Just as when the removal of the husk from rice grains is accomplished by threshing, the unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the performance of obligatory rites such as the *agnihotra* is not postulated as the cause of that removal of the husk;
likewise, the cessation of ignorance is also not postulated as the unseen result of the performance of obligatory rites.
Furthermore, we have already stated more than once that ritual actions are in contradiction with knowledge.

It has been stated that knowledge which is not in conflict with ritual actions is the cause for attaining the world of the gods, according to the Vedic scripture: "By knowledge, the world of the gods.

Furthermore, regarding the fruit to be postulated for the obligatory rites (nitya-karman) as they are heard in the scriptures, since that which is in conflict with ritual actions cannot be the effect of substances, qualities, or actions, what could possibly be postulated [as their fruit]?
Whether one assumes that result which is not seen to have efficacy in any action whatsoever, or rather that for which efficacy is observed and whose fruit is not contradicted by other actions—

if the fruit of action must necessarily be postulated to induce human activity, then, because the presumption based on scriptural implication (*śrutārthāpatti*) is exhausted regarding only those objects not contradicted by [other] actions, eternal liberation (*mokṣa*) cannot be postulated as the fruit.
Or rather, it is possible that there is the cessation of the ignorance regarding that obstruction,
because [this] is not contradictory and because its efficacy has been observed.
If it is argued that, by the logic of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), liberation alone must be postulated;
For indeed, all actions have a fruit, and no other fruit is conceivable apart from the fruits of those various actions;
and liberation remains as the residue,
which is accepted by the knowers of the Veda as the fruit [of knowledge].
If it is argued that therefore that [Self] alone must be postulated, we say no;

because the manifestations of the fruits of karma are infinite, the logic of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) is untenable. Indeed, no one who is not omniscient can determine the exact extent of the fruits of karma that fall within the scope of human desire.

Because the means for achieving those [ends], or the desires of persons, have no fixed place, time, or cause; and because the means for objects of human desire are impelled by the fruits desired by persons;
and because there is a diversity of desire in every living being, the infinity of fruits and their means is established.
Furthermore, because of that infinity, it is impossible for persons to know the full extent [of the means and results];
and if the full extent of the means and results is unknown, how can the exclusion of everything else establish liberation?
If it is argued that the exclusion refers to the results of karma, birth, and so forth; [we reply: no.
Even though the objects of desire and their means are infinite, the quality of being a result of karma is common to all of them.
Since liberation is not a result of karma, it would be the remainder;
therefore, if you argue that by the method of elimination (pariśeṣa) it is logical to postulate that [liberation] alone [is the result], we say: no.

If it is admitted that even this [result] is the fruit of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), then because it would logically follow that it belongs to the same genus as the fruits of other ritual acts, the "method of elimination" (*pariśeṣa*) becomes untenable.
Therefore, since the matter can be explained otherwise, the presumption based on scripture (*śrutārthāpatti*) is exhausted.

Since any one of the four types of results—origination (*utpatti*), acquisition (*āpti*), modification (*vikāra*), or purification (*saṃskāra*)—is possible as the fruit of obligatory rites, the presumption based on scripture is exhausted.
If it is argued that liberation is simply one of these four [states], we say no: first, it cannot be something produced, because it is eternal;
for this very reason, it is unchangeable and unconditioned.
And because it does not have the nature of a substance that serves as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
For a substance that possesses the nature of a means of accomplishment is what is consecrated (*saṃskriyate*),
such as a vessel or clarified butter (*ājya*) by means of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, it is neither something being conditioned nor something produced by conditioning, like a sacrificial post (yūpa) and so forth;
by process of elimination, it must be something to be attained (āpya).
Yet it cannot be attained, because its nature is that of the Self (ātman) and because it is one.

If it is argued that because the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) differ from other types of actions, their fruit must also be distinct from the fruits of those other actions—[we reply: no. Since they share the common characteristic of being "action" (*karmatva*), why should their fruit not be similar to the fruits of other actions? If it is argued that they differ due to a difference in their causal basis (*nimitta*), [we reply: no.
Because they are similar to the *kṣāmavatī* and other such rites;

for just as in the case of the *kṣāmavatī* sacrifice performed when a house has caught fire, or in other occasional rites (*naimittika*) such as "one offers when [the ladle] is broken" or "one offers when [the oblation] is spilled," liberation is not postulated as the fruit,
since these are distinguished by their status as occasional rites and because [the present texts] are heard to have occasions such as living as their cause.

Likewise, even for eternal things, liberation is not the result. Just as light serves as the means for all beings to perceive form, yet owls and the like do not see form by means of that light— because the eyes of owls and such are distinct from the eyes of other people— it is not postulated that the eyes of others have taste and so forth as their objects, since no capacity for such objects is observed in them.
Even if one travels very far, whatever capacity is observed in a particular domain, it is precisely there that some specific quality must be postulated.

As for what was said—that like poison mixed with spells, mantras, sugar, and so forth, or curd mixed with [neutralizing] substances, eternal things initiate other effects—let such a distinct effect be initiated; since this is desired, there is no contradiction.

There is no contradiction whatsoever in an action performed without ulterior motive (*nirabhisaṃdhi*), when conjoined with knowledge (*vidyā*), initiating a distinct and superior result. This is because a distinction is heard between the "sacrificer to the gods" (*devayājī*) and the "sacrificer to the Self" (*ātmayājī*) in such passages as "The sacrificer to the Self is superior," and "Whatever one performs with knowledge," and so forth.

As for the term *ātmayājī* mentioned by Manu in the context of the vision of the Supreme Self—specifically in the verse "One who sees equally is a sacrificer to the Self"—the meaning is that "one who sees equally becomes a sacrificer to the Self."
Alternatively, it is by way of what occurred in the past:
one performs the obligatory rites for the sake of self-sacrifice and self-purification, according to the Vedic revelation, "By this [rite], this limb of mine is purified.

Likewise, in the section beginning with "by the [rites] pertaining to the womb and those pertaining to gold," he shows that the purpose of the obligatory rites is the purification of the body and the instruments of action.
And he who is a "sacrificer to the Self" (*ātmayājī*) becomes capable of seeing those actions as equal;
for him, the vision of the Self arises as equal either in this life or in another birth. Seeing them as equal, he attains self-sovereignty (*svārājya*); such is the meaning.
The term "sacrificer to the Self," however, is employed by way of its former state.

This is for the purpose of demonstrating that actions performed constantly by those endowed with knowledge serve as the means for the arising of knowledge. Furthermore: "The wise say that Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—this is the supreme state characterized by sattva."
And thus, by means of the phrase "beyond the equality with the gods," it shows the dissolution of the elements: "one indeed goes to the five elements.
For those who read the text as "bhūtāny atyeti" (he transcends the elements), there is no fault, because their understanding regarding the Veda is limited.

Nor is this chapter merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), since it is seen to have the same purpose as both the *karmakāṇḍa* and the *upaniṣads*: namely, [the former] for the sake of the ripening of the fruits of actions ending with Brahmā, and [the latter] for the sake of the knowledge of the Self which is distinct from that.
Furthermore, because the performance of prescribed acts and the commission of prohibited acts are seen to result in fruits such as birth among stationary objects, horses, pigs, and so forth,
and because one observes pretas (hungry ghosts) such as those who eat vomit;
moreover, no actions can be understood by anyone as being either prescribed or prohibited apart from what is ordained or forbidden by the Śruti and Smṛti.

Since the fruits of action— such as rebirth as a ghost, a pig, or an immobile being— are perceived through both direct perception and inference for those who fail to perform prescribed duties and instead engage in prohibited ones,
and since no one admits that these are not the results of karma,

it should be understood that just as these states of ghosts, animals, and plants are the ripening of karma due to the non-performance of what is enjoined and the practice of what is forbidden, so too must the ripening of karma be recognized even in the case of exalted beings up to the level of Brahmā.
Therefore, [the passage] is not a non-factual explanatory statement (*abhūtārthavāda*), unlike such passages as "He extracted his own omentum" or "He wept.
If it is argued that even in those cases there should not be non-factual explanatory statements,
let it be so.
Nor does this much constitute a sublation of this principle, nor is our own position impaired,
nor can it be asserted that [the status of] "Brahmā, the creator of the universe," and so forth, is the fruit of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*).
Because the fruit of those [actions] has been stated to be equality with the gods (*devasārṣṭitā*),

therefore the fruits of constant rites (*nityakarman*) performed with a specific intention— such as the *Sarvamedha* and *Aśvamedha* sacrifices— are [attainments such as] the state of Brahman and so forth. However, for those [rites] which are constant, performed without intention, and intended for the purification of the self (*ātmasaṃskāra*), they serve the purpose of generating knowledge (*jñāna*).

Because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "this body is made brahmic," it is not contradictory that these [rites], by way of being indirect auxiliaries (ārādupakāraka), also become means for liberation;
we shall explain this point at the conclusion of the story of Janaka in the sixth [book].
As for what was said regarding [the Veda] being like poison, curd, and so forth, there is no contradiction because those things fall within the scope of perception and inference.

However, in the case of an object that is accessible solely through the word, if the sentence expressing that meaning does not exist, it is impossible to assume a similarity with poison, curd, and the like.
Furthermore, the authority of Śruti is not assumed in a domain where the subject matter contradicts other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as the statement, "Fire is cold and moistens."
But when that purpose is established by scripture (*śruti*), other means of knowledge become fallacious.

Just as in the cases "the firefly is fire" or "the sky is soiled," even though these are the perceptions of children, once it is ascertained that the other means of knowledge regarding those objects are true, the child's perception—even if its object was previously certain—becomes a fallacy.
Therefore, since the authority of the Veda is unerring, when that purpose is established, the sentence would possess such [authoritative] status.
But it is not due to human ingenuity;
for the sun does not fail to illuminate form because of human ingenuity.
Likewise, the sentences of the Veda do not have other meanings [than those derived from their own words].
Therefore, it is established that ritual actions do not have liberation as their purpose.
Consequently, this Brāhmaṇa section is commenced precisely to demonstrate that the fruits of action constitute *saṃsāra*.
Now, immediately after Jāratkāravas had ceased speaking, [the discussion continues].
Bhujyu Lāhyāyani—the son of Lāhya, whose name was Bhujyu—questioned him.
He said, "O Yājñavalkya. Thus, the vision of the Aśvamedha has been stated previously.
The horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha-kratu*), whether its fruit consists of both collective and individual results, or whether it is combined with knowledge or accomplished through knowledge alone,
represents the supreme pinnacle of all ritual actions.
For the traditional authorities remember that there is nothing greater than the killing of a fetus or the horse sacrifice among merits and demerits respectively;
by means of these, one attains both the totality (samaṣṭi) and the individual manifestations (vyaṣṭi).
Among these, the individual manifestations are well-known as pertaining to the interior of the cosmic egg and are the fruits resulting from the horse sacrifice.
It has been stated: "Death becomes its self; it becomes one among these deities" (1.2.7).
And death, characterized by hunger, is the collective intellect-self (*buddhyātman*), the first-born aggregate, the wind, the thread, the truth, Hiraṇyagarbha;
his manifested sphere of experience consists of all duality-and-unity, of which he is the essence.
He who is the inner self of all beings, the subtle mark whose essence is formless, upon whom depend the actions of all beings;
he who is the supreme goal and the ultimate fruit of actions and of the cognitions associated with those actions— how great is his range, how vast is his all-encompassing pervasion?
She should be questioned;
when she has been questioned, the entire sphere of bondage within saṃsāra will have been explained.
And, in order to demonstrate the world-transcending nature of that vision of the Self as both the aggregate and the individual, he relates his own personal narrative by way of a story.
And he thinks, "By this, I shall delude the intellect of the opponent.
Among the Madras— meaning in the country named Madra—
there were the Carakas, so called because they practiced vows for the sake of study, or alternatively, the Adhvaryus.
We wandered about; we traveled through the regions of Patañcala by name, of the Kāpya lineage, of the Kapiga gotra.
We went to his house.
He had a daughter who was possessed by a Gandharva—seized by some non-human being.
It is determined that the Gandharva is either Dhiṣṇya Agni (the sacrificial fire) or the presiding deity of the officiating priests, because of his distinguished knowledge.
For such a consciousness is not possible for mere reality alone.
Therefore, all of us, having surrounded him, asked: "Who are you? Who are you? What is your name? What is your true nature?"
That Gandharva replied: "I am Sudhanvan by name, Āṅgirasa by lineage.

When—at whatever time—we questioned him regarding the ends and limits of the worlds, we spoke to that Gandharva while all of us were boasting of ourselves, having set out to ascertain the dimensions of the cosmic egg."
We asked him: "How was it? Where were the Pārikṣitas?
And that Gandharva told us everything.
Therefore, this divine knowledge has been obtained by me;
you do not possess it,
and for that reason, you have been defeated.
This is the intended meaning:
"I, being endowed with knowledge and having received the traditional lore from a Gandharva, ask you, O Yājñavalkya: where did the Pārikṣitas go? What do you know of that?
O Yājñavalkya, tell me; I ask you: where did the Pārikṣitas go? //1//
He said: "He indeed spoke thus:
'They have surely gone to that place where those who perform the horse sacrifice go.'"
"Where indeed do those who have performed the horse sacrifice go? "This world extends for thirty-two days' journey by a divine chariot;
