the earth encircles it on all sides for twice that distance."
The ocean encircles that entire earth at twice its extent.
As wide as the edge of a razor or the wing of a fly is the space between them; having become a great bird (suparṇa) belonging to Indra, he gave them to Vāyu.
Vāyu, having placed them within himself, brought them to where those who had performed the horse sacrifice were.
In this very way, he indeed praised Vāyu alone; therefore, Vāyu is the individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*) and Vāyu is the collective manifestation (*samaṣṭi*).
He who knows this conquers recurrent death. Thereupon, Bhujyu Lāhyāyani desisted. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.3.2.
"He said"—Yājñavalkya said this.
The word "vai" is used for the purpose of recollection;
that Gandharva indeed said it to you.

"Where indeed, O Pārikṣitas, did they go?"—that is, "to where do those who perform the horse sacrifice go? When the question has been thus posed, he says: "Where, indeed—to what place—do those who perform the horse sacrifice go?"

With the intention of describing their movement, he states the measurement of the cosmic egg (bhuvanakośa): "Thirty-two, indeed, two more than thirty. That which is measured by the distance covered by the course of the divine chariot (devarathāhṛya)—the gods are the Ādityas, their chariot is the divine chariot; the measure of space delimited by the speed of that chariot is a "divine chariot-course" (devarathāhṛya). Thirty-two times that is the number of divine chariot-courses; such is its magnitude.
"That which is surrounded by the mountain Lokāloka;

where the body of Vairāja resides and where living beings experience the fruits of their karma—that is this world. This much is the world; beyond this is the non-world (aloka). That world is encircled on all sides by a perimeter whose extent is double the width of the expanse of the world."
The earth encircles and encompasses that world with such a measurement;
likewise, the ocean—which those versed in the ancient traditions call Ghanoda—encircles that earth on all sides with a measurement twice as great.
Therein, the measurement of the gap between the two halves of the cosmic eggshell is stated.

By which opening or path those who perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) go out and pervade the exterior— there, within the interval between the two halves of the cosmic egg, there is a space as large as the edge of the tip of a razor, or as subtle as the wing of a fly;
by that space, it is meant.

To those descendants of Parikṣit who had performed the horse sacrifice, the Supreme Lord— having become Suparṇa, the fire-altar built in the Aśvamedha, the subject of which was described by the passage beginning with "In the eastern quarter is his head"— and having thus become Suparṇa, the bird whose nature consists of wings,
tail, and so forth, gave them over to Vāyu; for, due to his embodied form, there is no movement for the Self in that state.
Having placed those Pārikṣitas within himself—having established them there and made them one with his own self—Vāyu led them to that place;
to where? To where the former Pārikṣitas who had performed the Aśvamedha sacrifices had gone.
Or rather, it was exactly thus that the Gandharva praised Vāyu alone as the goal of the Pārikṣitas.
The narrative is concluded.
Having emerged from the narrative, the Śruti now declares for our sake, by its own voice, the matter established by the narrative.

Since Vāyu is the inner self of all beings, both stationary and moving, and he alone is also their external self, therefore that which is the manifold pervasion (*vyāpti*)—existing as the adhyātma, adhibhūta, and adhidaiva—is Vāyu alone.
Likewise, the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*), in the form of the mere Sūtrātman, is Vāyu alone.
Thus, he who knows this approaches Vāyu as the Self, consisting of both the collective and individual forms.
"What is the fruit of that? he asked. [The answer is: "He conquers repeated death; having died once, he does not die again.
Then, because the question regarding the Self had been resolved, Bhuñyu Lāhyāyani ceased [inquiring]. 2.
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the third Adhyāya in the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya.
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1.
Then Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa questioned him.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all."
This is your self that is within all. That which breathes in by means of the out-breath (*prāṇa*) is your self that is within all;
that which breathes out by means of the in-breath (*apāna*) is your self that is within all.
He who breathes out with the vyāna breath—that is your self, dwelling within all.
He who breathes up with the udāna breath—that is your self, dwelling within all.
This is your self, dwelling within all.
Now, Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa questioned him.

It has been stated that one wanders through transmigratory existence, seized by the graspers (grahas) and over-graspers (atigrahas) impelled by merit and demerit, repeatedly abandoning and taking up those graspers and over-graspers.

Furthermore, the supreme excellence of merit—pertaining to the realm of the differentiated (vyākṛta), consisting of both the collective (samaṣṭi) and the individual (vyaṣṭi), and characterized by the attainment of the nature of both duality and unity)—has already been explained.

However, for one who is seized by the "seizers" (graha) and the "over-seizers" (atigraha) and thus transmigrates, the question of Uṣasta is now commenced in order to achieve the discernment of the Self itself—specifically, whether such a person exists or not, and what its characteristic is in the state of existence.

Through the realization of that Self, which is devoid of limiting adjuncts (nirupādhi), whose nature is free from action and its factors (kriyākāraka-vinirmukta-svabhāva), one is liberated from the aforementioned bondage along with its cause.
The connection of this narrative (ākhyāyikā) is well known.
Then Uṣasta by name, the son of Cakra (Cākrāyaṇa), questioned this very Yājñavalkya who was present there:
"That Brahman which is immediate— unmediated by anything from the perceiver— and direct—
not figurative like the 'Brahman that is the ear' and so forth."
What is that?
It is the Self (ātman).
By the word "Self," the inner self (pratyagātman) is meant.
In this context, because the word "self" (ātman) is well-known [to refer to Brahman],
the phrase "the innermost of all" (sarvasyābhyantaraḥ sarvāntaraḥ) refers to that self which is established by the two words "that" (yat) and "which" (yaḥ) as being Brahman;
[Nārada says] "explain that self to me."
"Speak clearly; just as one shows a cow by seizing it by the horn, say 'This is He'—that is the meaning.
Being addressed thus, Yājñavalkya replied: "Among these, Your Self is the innermost of all, existing within everything.
The term "innermost of all" is used for the purpose of perceiving [the Self] through all its specific attributes.
That which is directly perceived, immediate, non-figurative, the supreme Brahman, the greatest, the Self of all that is within—all these qualities combined describe this very one.
Who is this Self of yours?
It is that by which this aggregate of causes and effects (the body) is possessed of a self; that is your Self.
The meaning is: "of your aggregate of body and organs.

In that regard, there is the physical mass (piṇḍa), within it the subtle body (liṅgātman) which is the aggregate of organs—the third—and that which is being doubted: "Which among these is intended by you as my innermost Self? To this, the other replied: "That which [is associated] with breath (prāṇa), which moves through the mouth and nose..."

It breathes, meaning it performs the activity of breathing; that by which the vital breath (prāṇa) is led forth is its meaning. That is your self (ātman), consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya), belonging to your aggregate of body and organs.
The rest is the same [as before].
"He who breathes out with the out-breath (apāna) and breathes across with the diffused-breath (vyāna)"— the lengthening [of the vowels] is a Vedic archaism.
By whom all activities, such as breathing and so forth, belonging to the aggregate of causes and effects, are performed, just like those of a wooden machine.
For vital functions such as breathing do not exist in that which is not presided over by something possessing consciousness, just like a wooden machine.
Therefore, being presided over by the "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya), which is distinct [from the body], it undergoes vital functions such as breathing, like a wooden machine.
Consequently, there exists that which is distinct from the aggregate of the body and its instruments, and which exercises this governance. //1//
Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa said: "Just as one might say, 'This is a cow,' or 'This is a horse,' so too has this been pointed out.
Please explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, the Self that is within all."
"This is your Self, which is within all. "Which one, Yājñavalkya, is within all?
"You would not see the seer of seeing."
You would not hear the hearer of hearing;
you would not think the thinker of thought; you would not discern the discerner of discernment.
"This is your Self that is within all; everything else but this is afflicted.
Thereupon, Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa ceased questioning.
Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa said: "Just as someone, having first made one promise, might later speak otherwise because he has contradicted himself—

just as one might first promise, 'I shall show you this cow' or 'this horse,' and then later point it out by means of signs such as its moving or running— in the same way, this Brahman has been pointed out by you through signs such as breathing and so forth."
"What is the use of much talk? Setting aside the pretext of the thirst for water, explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, the Self that is within all.
The other replied, "I shall indeed follow through on my initial promise that your Self is distinct [from the body]."
That is exactly as I have stated.
As for what was further said—that one should make that self an object of cognition like a jar or other things—that is not done because it is impossible.
But why is it impossible?
He said:
"Because of the intrinsic nature of things.
But what, then, is this intrinsic nature of things?
The state of being the seer of seeing and so forth:
for the Self is indeed the seer of seeing.
Seeing is of two kinds: worldly and ultimate.
In this context, the worldly function of the internal organ associated with the eye is produced;
thus it is born and it perishes.
However, that which is the vision of the Self—like the heat and light of fire—is not born and does not perish, because it is the very nature of the Seer.

That [Self], being associated with the vision that is produced and serves as a limiting adjunct (upādhi), is designated as "the seer" and appears as if distinct, such that one says "the seer" and "vision.

This worldly vision, which arises colored by form through the gateway of the eyes, is born as if already conjoined with the eternal vision of the Self; it is born as if pervaded by its reflection, and likewise perishes. Therefore, the Self is figuratively called "the seer" at all times.
Even while seeing, one both sees and does not see;
yet there is never any alteration whatsoever in the vision of the Seer.
And so it will be stated in the sixth chapter: "It meditates, as it were; it vibrates, as it were."
And [the scripture] says: "For there is no loss of the vision of the seer.
Regarding this meaning, it is said: you would not see the seer—who is the agent pervading his own eternal vision—with respect to that worldly vision which has become an object.
That worldly vision, having become an object, is colored by form and manifests form; it does not pervade the inner Self (pratyak), who is its own pervader.
Therefore, you should not see that inner Self as the seer of the seeing;
likewise, you should not hear it as the hearer of the hearing;
likewise, you should not conceive of it as the pervader of pure mental activity, which is the function of the mind.
Likewise, you would not perceive the pervader of pure consciousness, which is a mere modification of the intellect;
this is the very nature of reality, and therefore it cannot be shown like a cow or other such objects.
Regarding the phrase "the seer of seeing," some explain the words differently.
One should not perceive the seer of seeing—the agent of seeing—without making a distinction between [the act of] seeing; one should not perceive the agent of mere seeing.
In the word "dṛṣṭeḥ," the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
That seeing, while being performed, becomes an object like a jar.
By using the form *draṣṭāram* ending in the suffix *-tṛ*, [the author] expresses that the seer is the agent of seeing.
Therefore, the intention of the commentators is that "he is the seer of seeing" means he is the agent of seeing.

In this regard, they do not perceive the fault that the mention of "seeing" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*) in the genitive case is redundant; or, even if they do perceive it, they show no concern for it, regarding it as either a tautology, a lack of substance, or a careless reading.
But how can there be redundancy? Since the agency of seeing is already established by the suffix *-tṛ* itself, the word "of seeing" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*) is superfluous;
in that case, one should have said only "one would not see the seer. For it is traditionally taught that the suffix *-tṛ* occurs after a verbal root to denote the agent of the meaning of that root.
For this much alone is expressed by the word: "it leads the goer" or "it leads the eater.
However, one should not employ such expressions as "the goer of going" or "the cutter of cutting" when no specific meaning [beyond the agent] exists.
Nor should it be discarded as a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) when a valid meaning is possible.
Nor is this a case of a faulty recitation, because there is no disagreement among all [the traditions].
Therefore, it is only the weakness of the intellect of the commentators, not a lapse on the part of the students; rather, it is as we have explained.

Having distinguished [the Self] from the worldly view, the Self must be shown as characterized by the eternal vision; thus, the twofold use of the word "vision" (dṛṣṭi) as a qualifier of both the agent and the object is justified for the purpose of determining the true nature of the Self.
Furthermore, this is consistent with the syntactic unity of the sentence in another passage: "For there is no cessation of the vision of the seer."
And thus, its syntactic unity with another scriptural passage—“The eyes see” and “This ear has heard”—is established.
This is also supported by logic.

For in this way alone is the eternity of the Self established; otherwise, it would be contradictory to say that the Self is eternal while being subject to modification, since that which undergoes modification cannot be eternal.

The words of the Śruti—“It meditates, as it were; it trembles, as it were,” “For there is no loss of the vision of the seer,” and “This is the eternal greatness of the Brāhmaṇa”—do not admit of any other interpretation.
[Objection: But do not such words as “the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower” also fail to apply to the unchanging nature of the Self? [Reply:
No, for those are merely restatements of worldly usage as it is commonly found.
Those [passages] are not intended for the determination of the nature of the Self;
rather, because it is impossible for "the seer of seeing" and so forth to have any other meaning, their purpose is understood to be exactly as stated.

Therefore, it is solely due to a lack of understanding that the qualification has been discarded; for since "the seer of seeing" and so forth cannot possibly have any other meaning, their purpose is understood to be exactly as stated.
Therefore, it was precisely due to a lack of understanding that the qualification "of perception" was omitted.
This Self of yours is qualified by all the aforementioned qualifications.
Hence, anything other than this Self—whether it be the body as an effect or the subtle body (liṅga) consisting of the instruments—is subject to suffering.
"This alone is the one that is unafflicted, indestructible, and immutable.
Thereupon, Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa desisted from questioning. //2//
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the third Adhyāya in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya.
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1.
Then Kahola Kauṣītakeya questioned him: "O Yājñavalkya," he said, "explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all."
"This is your Self that is within all. "Which one, Yājñavalkya, is within all?
"It is that which transcends hunger and thirst, grief and delusion, old age and death."
Having indeed known this Self, the Brahmins rise above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and then lead the life of a mendicant.
For the desire for sons is the same as the desire for wealth, and the desire for wealth is the same as the desire for worlds;
for both of these are indeed merely desires.
Therefore, a Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship, should seek to abide in childlike simplicity;
and having become disillusioned with both childlike simplicity and scholarship, he is then a sage;
and having become disillusioned with both non-sagehood and sagehood, he is then a true Brahmin.
"By what means would he be a Brahmin? He would be exactly such as he is by that [means]. Anything other than this is afflicted.
Thereupon, Kahola Kauṣītakeya ceased questioning.
The bondage along with its cause has been explained;
the existence of that which is bound, as well as its distinctness [from the body], has also been established.
Now, the means for its liberation from bondage—namely, the knowledge of the Self accompanied by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*)—must be stated; thus the question of Kahola begins: "Now..."
Kahola, by name, the son of Kuṣītaka (Kauṣītakeya), questioned him, saying, "O Yājñavalkya," as before:
"Explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all,
knowing which one is liberated from bondage."
Yājñavalkya said: "This is your Self.
Now, was one and the same Self questioned by both Uṣasta and Kahola, or were two distinct Selves with identical characteristics asked about?
It is more reasonable that they were distinct, since it is thus that the non-redundancy of the two questions is logically established.

For if indeed one and the same Self were intended in the two questions of Uṣasta and Kahola, then since it would have been understood by one question alone, a second question concerning that same subject would be purposeless;
nor is the sentence of the nature of a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
Therefore, some explain that these two selves—the individual knower (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman)—are distinct.
That is not so,
because of the promise "that [is it]";
for in the reply, "This is your Self," that very thing was promised.
Furthermore, it is not possible for a single aggregate of causes and effects to possess two selves;
for a single aggregate of causes and effects possesses a self through only one self.
Moreover, the self of Uṣasta is not different from the self of Kahola, nor is there any self distinct from it by way of its essential nature.
Because it is impossible for two things to be non-figurative, the Self, and the innermost of all;
for if one among the two is the non-figurative Brahman, the other must necessarily be figurative, as must be the case with their being the Self and the innermost of all,
since the referents of these terms are mutually exclusive.

If the one Brahman-Ātman that is within all is the primary [reality], there must necessarily be another, non-all-pervading non-Ātman that is not primary. Therefore, the repetition of the description of the one [Brahman] is intended to specify its particular qualities. As for that which was stated in the second question—being identical to what was previously mentioned—that is merely a restatement of the former, intended to express some specific quality of that very same [Brahman] which had not yet been stated.
What, then, is this distinction?
It is said: in the first question, it was stated that there exists a distinct Self to which this bondage, along with its cause, belongs;
in the second, however, the distinction stated is that very same Self's transcendence of the attributes of transmigratory existence, such as hunger and so forth.

Because one is liberated from the aforementioned bondage through the thorough knowledge of its specific nature combined with renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), therefore the question and its answer—ending with the words "This is your Self"—possess an identical meaning. Now, an objection may be raised: how can there be a coexistence of contradictory attributes in a single Self, such as being beyond hunger and so forth, and yet possessing those very same qualities? This is not so.

Because it has been refuted. For we have stated more than once, in the course of explaining contradictory scriptural passages, that the state of being a transmigrating being is merely an illusion produced by contact with the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of the aggregate characterized by the performance of the functions of name-and-form (nāmarūpa-vikāra-kārya-karaṇa).

Just as a rope, a mother-of-pearl shell, the sky, and so forth, appear as a snake, silver, or impurity when characterized by attributes superimposed by another, yet in themselves they are merely the rope, the mother-of-pearl shell, the sky, and so on;
and thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that objects possess a coexistence of contradictory attributes.

If it be argued that the existence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as name and form would contradict such scriptural passages as "One only, without a second" and "There is no diversity here at all," we say: no.
This has already been resolved by the analogy of foam on water and by the analogies of clay and so forth.

However, when name and form are examined from the perspective of ultimate reality as being distinct from the true nature of the Supreme Self according to the scriptures, they do not exist in reality as separate entities, just like the modifications of clay and the like, or like the modifications of foam and jars upon water; at that time, with reference to that [reality], it is said: "One only, without a second," and "not here..."
It attains the status of being the object of the vision of ultimate reality (paramārtha) through such [scriptural passages] as "There is no diversity whatsoever.

However, when the nature of Brahman— which, like the nature of a rope, a mother-of-pearl shell, or the sky, exists in its own form and remains untouched by anything— even while being untouched by its own essence, is not distinguished from the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of the body and organs produced by name and form due to innate ignorance (avidyā), [it is not realized].
And when the perception of the limiting adjuncts of name and form (*nāmarūpa-upādhi*) no longer occurs naturally, then this entire conventional usage regarding the existence of other entities ceases.

This false conventional usage based on differentiation exists for those who hold that an entity exists as something distinct from the reality of Brahman, and it does not exist for those [who hold otherwise].

However, when the proponents of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-vādin*) investigate the thing-in-itself in accordance with the scriptures, they conclude: "Does an entity truly exist or not? [The answer is: Brahman alone is non-dual and devoid of all conventional usage."
Therefore, no contradiction whatsoever is established;

for we do not admit the existence of any other entity when one is intent upon the definitive determination of ultimate reality, according to the scriptural testimony: "One alone, without a second," and "Without interior or exterior."

Nor is it denied that at the time of the conventional usage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there is no conventional discourse regarding action, agent, fruit, and so forth for those who lack discrimination.
Therefore, with respect to both knowledge and ignorance, all conventional discourse—whether pertaining to the knower or to the world—is established.
Consequently, there is no ground for any suspicion of contradiction.
For all proponents [of philosophical systems], the conventional discourse established by ultimate reality and worldly convention is unavoidable.

In that regard, with reference to the nature of the self as ultimate reality, the question is asked again: "O Yājñavalkya, which is the innermost of all? The other replies: "That which is free from hunger and thirst."

The desire to eat is hunger (*aśanāyā*), and the desire to drink is thirst (*pipāsā*). The connection with what follows is: "he who transcends that hunger and thirst. Just as the sky, though perceived by the undiscriminating as if it were covered by a surface and impurity, transcends that surface and impurity because, in the ultimate sense, its nature is not conjoined with them, so too [the Self transcends hunger and thirst].

Similarly, although Brahman—which is characterized by freedom from hunger, thirst, and so forth—is being approached by the deluded, they nevertheless transcend it [in their experience] through such thoughts as "I am hungry" and "I am thirsty," because its essential nature is in reality unassociated with those states.
This is according to the Śruti: "It is not tainted by the suffering of the world, being external to it.
The meaning is: by the suffering superimposed upon it by the ignorant world.
Because hunger and thirst share the single characteristic of being functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), they are treated as a compound.
"Grief" (*śoka*) refers to desire (*kāma*);
for one who broods over a desired object, that lack of contentment which arises is the seed of desire in one overcome by craving, for by means of it desire is kindled.
Delusion (*moha*), however, is a confusion consisting of non-discrimination produced by erroneous cognition;
it is ignorance (*avidyā*), the seed from which all misfortune springs.
Because their functions are distinct, sorrow (*śoka*) and delusion (*moha*) are not compounded into a single term.
With the mind as their locus,
and likewise with the body as their locus, those two transcend old age and death.
"Old age" refers to the transformation of the aggregate of the body and its organs, characterized by signs such as wrinkles and grey hair.
"Death" refers to the cessation of that [existence], ending in transformation.
One transcends those two—old age and death—which have the body as their locus.

Those states beginning with hunger, which have the vital breath, the mind, and the body as their locus, and which occur incessantly among living beings like days and nights or like the waves of the ocean, are called "saṃsāra" (transmigration) among living beings.
That Self which is characterized as "the seer of seeing," and so forth— direct, immediate, non-figurative, and the innermost of all—
is never touched by the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and thirst, extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass,
just as the sky is not touched by impurities such as clouds.

Having known and realized this very Self, which is one's own true nature—thinking, "I am this Supreme Brahman, eternally liberated from all saṃsāra and ever-content"—the Brāhmaṇas [attain liberation].
The mention of "Brāhmaṇas" is because the qualification for renunciation (*vyutthāna*) belongs to Brāhmaṇas alone;
thus, having renounced—that is, having risen by turning away from worldly life—they attain liberation.

To the question "Why?", he says: "The desire for a son" (*putraiṣaṇā*) means the seeking of things for the sake of a son. It is the seeking directed toward a son as a means for conquering this world, in the thought, "May I conquer this world through a son. This refers to the taking of a wife; the meaning is that [one should renounce] without having taken a wife.

And there is the acquisition of cattle and other means for performing rituals, which serve as instruments for action, with the thought: "Having performed this rite, I shall conquer the world of the ancestors. Or else, by means of knowledge joined with ritual action, one seeks the world of the gods; or by means of divine wealth alone—that is, the knowledge of Hiraṇyagarbha—one seeks the world of the gods.
Some maintain that there is no renunciation at all of such divine wealth.
Because it is said that emergence [from samādhi] occurs by means of its power—that is incorrect;
for among the types of desire, divine wealth is indeed included in the scriptural reading: "Desire is of this extent."
Knowledge whose object is deities such as Hiraṇyagarbha is called "citta," because it is the cause for attaining the world of the gods;
for the knowledge of Brahman, which has as its object the undifferentiated mass of pure consciousness free from all limiting adjuncts, is not a cause for attaining the world of the gods.

"Therefore all that became this," and "for he becomes the Self of these," according to the Śruti; for by its power alone there is emergence [from the state of ignorance], as indicated by the specific statement: "Having known this very Self."

Therefore, having risen above these three objects of desire—which are the means for attaining the non-Self world—the meaning is that one should not form a craving (*tṛṣṇā*) for this threefold means of attaining the non-Self world; for the scripture states: "Desire is indeed of this extent. Desire is *eṣaṇā*. Thus, the sense is that one should not harbor thirst for these three types of means to worldly existence.
For every desire for means is indeed a desire for the fruit;
therefore, he explains: "This very seeking is but one seeking.
How so? For that which is the seeking of sons is the same as the seeking of wealth.
Because they are equal in being means for attaining visible results:
whatever is the desire for wealth (*vittaiṣaṇā*), that is the desire for the world (*lokaiṣaṇā*), for it is solely for the sake of a result.
Indeed, everyone who is impelled by the aim of a result takes up every means thereto.

Therefore, this is but a single desire; that which is the desire for worldly objects (*loka-eṣaṇā*) cannot be accomplished without means, and thus, because of the distinction between the goal and the means, both of these are indeed desires.
Consequently, for the knower of Brahman, there is neither ritual action nor any means for ritual action.

Therefore, those Brāhmaṇas who have transcended all ritual action and all means for ritual action—including the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth, which are intended for the gods, the ancestors, and men—for by means of that [thread], one performs actions pertaining to the gods, the ancestors, and men.
This is established by such scriptural passages as, "The *nivīta* [mode] is for human beings.

Therefore, the Brāhmaṇas who know Brahman, having previously renounced ritual actions and the instruments of action such as the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth, enter upon the state of the Paramahaṃsa wandering mendicant and practice the life of a mendicant (*bhikṣācarya*). "Bhikṣācarya" means wandering for the sake of alms.

They wander about, having abandoned the external marks prescribed by the Smṛtis, for those who take refuge in the mere stage of life (āśrama) alone have as their means of livelihood the outward appearance of a wandering mendicant (parivrājya). Thus it is said: "One should pierce through [the world] while being devoid of marks," and from such Smṛti texts as: "Therefore, the knower of Dharma is without marks, with unmanifested marks, and of unmanifested conduct."

This is because of such scriptural passages as, “Then the wandering mendicant, wearing discolored garments, shaven-headed, without possessions,” and so forth, and also, “Having shaved off his hair including the top-knot, and having cast away the sacred thread.

Now, one might object: since the statement, “Having renounced, they then lead the life of a mendicant,” is a description in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*), this is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) and not an injunction; for no injunctive suffix—whether it be the optative (*liṅ*), the imperative (*loṭ*), or the gerundive (*tavya*)—is heard here.

Therefore, it is not possible to effect the abandonment of the means of practice—such as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth—which are enjoined by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, on the basis of mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). One should study, officiate at sacrifices, or sacrifice only while wearing the sacred thread. Indeed, even in the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), study is enjoined: "By renouncing the Veda one becomes a Śūdra; therefore, one should not renounce the Veda."

And Āpastamba says: "One should indeed release one's speech only during Vedic recitation. Furthermore: "Neglecting the Veda, reviling the Veda, giving false testimony, killing a friend, eating forbidden food or drink, and drinking liquor—these six are equal [in gravity]."
Thus, because the fault of abandoning the Vedas is heard [in scripture],

and because among the duties of a wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) it is stated: "One should wear the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta) during the service of gurus, elders, guests, at the fire-oblation (homa), in the rites of recitation (japa), while eating, when sipping water (ācamana), and during Vedic study (svādhyāya)," [the wearing of the thread is required].

Since actions are enjoined as duties to be performed in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, and since the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) is prescribed as an ancillary part of the service to one's guru and others, its abandonment cannot be understood [to be intended].

Even though renunciation from desires is indeed enjoined, it is nevertheless a renunciation only from the three desires for son, wealth, and worlds, and not a renunciation of all action and the means of action.

Furthermore, in the case of abandoning everything, that which was not prescribed would have been performed, and that which was prescribed—such as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth—would have been discarded.
Thus, a great transgression would be committed, caused by the non-performance of what is enjoined and the performance of what is prohibited.
Therefore, the abandonment of the signs such as the sacred thread is merely a blind tradition. [Reply: No.
“For the ascetic (yati), all that—namely the sacred thread and the Vedas—he should abandon,” according to the Śruti.
Furthermore, because every Upaniṣad has as its ultimate goal the knowledge of the Self, for it begins with the injunction:

“The Self is to be seen, heard, and reflected upon. And that very Self is to be known as such: immediate, non-mediated, the innermost of all, and devoid of the transmigratory attributes such as hunger and so forth.
This much is well-established:

since this entire Upaniṣad has such a purpose, it cannot be a subordinate element of another injunction; therefore, it is not a mere explanatory passage (arthavāda), because the knowledge of the Self is something to be performed.
Furthermore, since the Self does not possess attributes such as hunger and so forth, it must be understood as distinct from both the means of action and their results.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) consists in knowing the Self through non-discrimination [from these].

This is established by such scriptural passages as: “He who thinks ‘that one is one and I am another’ does not know”; “He goes from death to death who perceives here any kind of diversity”; “It should be viewed as one alone”; “One only, without a second”; and “That thou art.”
The fruit of action and the means of attainment—being other than the Self which transcends the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and so forth—fall within the domain of ignorance.

This is established by hundreds of scriptural passages such as: "For where there is, as it were, duality," "He does not know, thinking 'He is one and I am another,'" and "But those who know otherwise than this.
Furthermore, knowledge and ignorance cannot coexist in a single person because of their mutual contradiction, just like darkness and light.
Therefore, for the knower of the Self, no qualification belonging to the domain of ignorance—consisting of the distinctions between action, agent, and fruit—is to be regarded as valid;
for such things are censured in passages such as, "He goes from death to death.
Furthermore, all means of action and their fruits, being within the domain of ignorance, are intended to be abandoned by the knowledge of the Self, which is the opposite of that ignorance.
And because the means such as the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) have that [worldly life] as their object;
therefore, this desire, which has as its object something other than the Self—which is by nature neither a means nor a fruit—is distinct [from those two].
For both of these desires consist precisely of means and fruits.
Because the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth, as well as the rituals to be accomplished by them, serve as means;
and because of the restrictive statement using the word "for" (*hi*), which declares that "both these are indeed desires";

therefore, since they consist of means such as the sacred thread and the rituals to be accomplished by them, and because they fall within the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*), taking the form of desire, and being of a nature to be abandoned, renunciation (*vyutthāna*) from them is precisely what is intended to be enjoined.

[Objection: But surely, since the Upaniṣads have as their primary purpose the knowledge of the Self, the scriptural statement regarding renunciation (*vyutthāna*) is for the sake of praising that [knowledge], not an injunction.
[Reply: No; because we hear of a common agent with the knowledge that is intended to be enjoined.
For it is never possible in the Veda to hear of a common agency between that which is not to be performed and that which is to be performed.

For just as there is an audition of the pressing, the offering, and the consumption as things to be performed— namely, "having pressed, having offered, they consume"— in the same way, there would be an audition of the knowledge of the Self, the renunciation of desires, and the life of mendicancy as things to be performed, sharing a common agent.

If it is argued that the abandonment of the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) and other such items follows as a matter of course from the injunction to know the Self— since they fall within the domain of ignorance and constitute objects of craving, and thus need not be separately enjoined—

it is even more strongly established by the very injunction to know the Self that this abandonment is indeed intended; for its firmness is secured by the scriptural teaching that it shares the same agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) as that injunction.
The same applies to the practice of begging for alms.
As for the objection that, because it is stated as a description of the present, it is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda)—this is not so;
there is no fault, because it is similar to injunctions such as that regarding the sacrificial post made of Udumbara wood.
By the statement, "Having emerged [from meditation], they wander for alms," the state of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is enjoined;
and in the stage of wandering mendicancy, the sacrificial thread and other such implements are prescribed by both Śruti and Smṛti as well as the characteristic marks (liṅga).

If it is argued that, having excluded that [first stage], there is an emergence from another [stage] even while still characterized by seeking (*eṣaṇā*), we say no. This is because a different form of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) arises from that mendicancy characterized by emergence from seeking which has the same agent as knowledge (*vijñāna*).
For that mendicancy characterized by emergence from seekings is an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of the Self.
Because it consists in the renunciation of desires that are opposed to the knowledge of the Self,
and because desire has ignorance as its object,
there exists a form of the life-stage distinct from those [other stages], namely the wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya), which is the means for attaining results such as the world of Brahman.

Since the injunctions regarding the means such as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and the injunctions regarding the [specific] marks (*liṅga*) have as their object that which is undertaken by way of the means consisting of seeking (*eṣaṇā*),

it is not proper to subvert the knowledge of the Self— which is enjoined in all the Upaniṣads— merely because of the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*) when the scope for renunciation (*pārivrājya*) exists within that context.

Furthermore, when there is a desire to acquire the means for the sphere of ignorance— such as the sacrificial thread and other such things, which consist of the pursuit of objects of desire— the realization "I am Brahman," which is by nature neither a means nor a fruit and is devoid of the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger, is necessarily sublated; yet such sublation is not tenable, because all the Upaniṣads have that [realization] as their sole purpose.
If it is argued that the Vedic scripture, by enjoining the practice of begging for alms (*bhikṣācarya*), contradicts itself;

or even if it were so, that having prescribed the renunciation of all desires, it then enjoins a portion of those very desires—namely, the practice of begging for alms—and thereby implies other things connected to them;
we say no, because begging for alms is not the primary motive, as one eats only after having performed the oblation.
For that [the begging of alms] is not the motive, since it is a subsidiary act of performance;
it might even be something that does not effect a refinement (asaṃskāra),
but it is certainly not the practice of begging for alms.
For even the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from observances (*niyama*) is undesirable to one who knows Brahman.

If it is asked, "If the unseen merit of observances is undesirable, what is the purpose of wandering for alms?"—the answer is no; because renunciation from other means of accomplishment has been prescribed.
If it is asked, "Even so, what is the use of that?"—
if it were to exist, we certainly accept it;
for there are indeed statements prescribed regarding the life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya), such as "One should study while wearing the sacred thread," and so forth.
It has been refuted that those [scriptural passages] refer merely to the wandering life of one who lacks knowledge;
for it has been stated that otherwise there would be a contradiction with the knowledge of the Self:
"One who is free from desire, free from undertaking, free from salutation, and free from praise..."
"The gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa who, though his karma is exhausted, remains unexhausted [in spirit]"—thus the Smṛti shows the absence of all action for the knower;
and also [the text] says, "The knower is one who has cast off marks and knows Dharma.
Therefore, the knower of the Self should undertake the state of the Paramahaṃsa wandering mendicant alone, characterized by renunciation and consisting in the abandonment of all means of action.

Because the ancient Brahmins, having realized this Self to be by nature devoid of means and fruits, renounced all that is characterized by desire— consisting of the nature of means and fruits— and wandered as mendicants,
abandoning both action for the sake of seen and unseen ends and its instruments;
therefore, even today, a Brahmin who knows Brahman [should abandon] scholarship, which is the state of being a scholar.
This knowledge of the Self is "pāṇḍitya" (scholarship).

Having become weary of [the world] and having known it completely—that is, having made the knowledge of the Self exhaustive by means of both the teacher and the traditional scripture—one rises above the desires (*eṣaṇā*). For that scholarship culminates precisely in rising above desires, because it arises from the rejection of desires and is opposed to them.

Indeed, the renunciation of desires is not enjoined by the knowledge of the Self alone; rather, it is firmly established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the use of the suffix denoting common agency (*samāna-kartṛkatva*) and by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Therefore, having renounced desires, one should "wish to abide" (*tiṣṭhāset*) in a state of "childhood" (*bālya*), which consists in the possession of knowledge. For strength, for others who do not know the Self, consists in relying upon means and results.

Abandoning that [empirical] strength, the wise man should rely solely on the strength of the realization of the Self—which is by nature devoid of means and fruits—and upon that state alone; for when he relies on that, the organs are no longer able to carry him away and establish him in the objects of desire. Indeed, it is the fool, who is bereft of the strength of knowledge, that the organs compel toward the pursuit of objects, both seen and unseen.
"Strength" (bala) means the setting aside of all objective perceptions through self-knowledge;
therefore, one should remain in that state of "childlike innocence" (bālya).
Thus, it is said in another Vedic text: "By means of the Self, one finds vigor."
And it is said: "This Self is not to be attained by one who is devoid of strength.
Having completely mastered both childhood and scholarship, and having become a sage (*muni*) through reflection, one becomes a yogi;
this much indeed is to be accomplished by a Brahmin.
Namely, the complete setting aside of all notions of self and its objects;
having accomplished this, the yogi becomes one who has fulfilled his task.

And having thoroughly completed both non-silence—the knowledge of the Self—and the setting aside of notions of self and its objects, which are designated as "wisdom" and "childlike innocence," [he attains the goal].
Silence (*mauna*) is the ultimate fruit of the rejection of the notion that there is anything other than the Self;

and having become disillusioned with that, one becomes a *brāhmaṇa* who has accomplished his task, for the realization arises that "Brahman alone is everything. He is a *brāhmaṇa* who has accomplished his task.
Therefore, O Brāhmaṇa, his status as a Brāhmaṇa has indeed been attained in its non-figurative sense; by what [means] would he be a Brāhmaṇa, and by what conduct would he become one?

"By whatever conduct one may be, by that very [conduct] he is such as this"—meaning, by whatever kind of conduct one may be, by that very [conduct] one becomes a *brāhmaṇa* possessing the aforementioned characteristics.
The phrase "by whatever kind of conduct" is for the purpose of praise; it is this state of being a *brāhmaṇa* that is being praised.
But there is no disregard for the practice [of the means].

Therefore, from this state of Brahmanhood—which is the nature of the Self transcending hunger and so forth, and which is eternally satisfied—there is another entity, characterized by desire, which is the object of ignorance;
it is afflicted, perishable, and seized by suffering.
"It is essence-less, like a dream, an illusion, or a mirage;
the Self alone is one, absolute, and eternally liberated. Thereupon, Kahola Kaupatakeya ceased questioning. //1//

The text beginning from the Śākalya Brāhmaṇa is commenced for the purpose of attaining knowledge of the true nature of that Brahman which was described as being directly perceived, not hidden, and the Self within all;
for the elements beginning with earth and ending with space are established in a relationship of interiority and exteriority.

Having negated whatever is external among those [layers], after reaching what is beyond the external, the Seer—the innermost Self, non-figurative, and free from all the attributes of transmigratory existence—is to be shown; such is the beginning [of this section]:
Then Gārgī Vācaknavī questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," she said, "..."

"Gārgī, do not ask beyond this!

Then Gārgī by name,
the daughter of Vācaknu,
questioned him; she said, "O Yājñavalkya."
That is to say, this entire collection of earthly elements is woven warp and woof within the waters;
"woven" means like the long threads of a cloth, and "woof" means like the crosswise threads—or conversely—meaning it is pervaded on all sides, both internally and externally, by the waters.
Otherwise, it would fall apart like a handful of flour.

This, first of all, is the inference presented: that which is an effect, being delimited and gross, is pervaded by a cause that is undelimited and subtle; this is observed, for example, as the earth is pervaded by water.
In the same way, each preceding element must be pervaded by each succeeding one that is more pervasive.

Thus, this is the meaning of the question concerning the Self that is within all. In that regard, the five elements exist only as a composite, established in a progressively subtler state, as the pervasive, and as the causal form; and there is no other entity whatsoever apart from the Supreme Self, in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "The Truth of truth."
The five elements are truth, and the Supreme Self is the truth of truth.
Now, in what indeed are the waters woven like warp and woof? Since they too are effects, gross, and limited, they must exist somewhere in a state of being woven as warp and woof;
in what, then, is their state of being woven?
In this way, the connection with each successive moment must be applied.
[Gārgī asks: "In the wind, O Yājñavalkya? [The opponent objects: "Should it not rather be said, 'In fire'?"

This is not a fault; for fire does not attain its own existence independently like the other elements, without depending on an earthly or watery substrate. Therefore, the state of being woven across and through it is not taught [in that manner]. [Gārgī asks: "In what, then, is air woven across and through? [Yājñavalkya replies: "In the worlds of the atmosphere, Gārgī. Those very elements, when combined, constitute the worlds of the atmosphere.
Those [worlds] also [are merged] in the worlds of the Gandharvas;
the worlds of the Gandharvas in the worlds of the Ādityas;
and the worlds of the Ādityas in the worlds of the Moon.
The worlds of the moon [are merged] into the worlds of the stars; the worlds of the stars into the worlds of the gods;
the worlds of the gods into the worlds of Indra.
The worlds of Indra consist of those beings that originate the body of Virāj; the worlds of Prajāpati consist of those beings that originate the world of Prajāpati;
and the so-called worlds of Brahmā consist of those beings that originate the cosmic egg.

For everywhere, the elements, having combined and transformed into the form of the support for the enjoyment of the objects to be attained, exist according to a sequence of subtle degrees; it is these very five that are referred to by the plural number [in the term *bhūtāni*].
As for the question, "In what, indeed, are the worlds of Brahmā woven to and across?"—Yājñavalkya said: "O Gārgī, do not ask beyond your own question.
The meaning is: do not ask about the deity who must be known through scripture (*āgama*) by means of inference (*anumāna*), thereby overstepping the proper method of inquiry.
And as she was questioning me, your head— your skull— would have clearly fallen off;
for the domain of a deity's own question is the field of scripture,
and Gārgī’s question has overstepped that domain of questioning.

Because it is inferential, that deity regarding whom the question is asked is "one whose questioning is excessive" (*atipraśnyā*); [a deity] who is not excessively questionable is "not excessively questionable" (*anatipraśnyā*),
meaning she is limited solely to the scope of her own questions.
The meaning is that it is to be known solely through scripture;
you are questioning too far about that deity which should not be questioned beyond this. Therefore, Gārgī, do not question further.
"If you do not wish to die, then stop.
Thereupon Gārgī Vācaknavī ceased questioning. //1//

Now, since the most internal thread (*sūtra*) of the worlds of Brahman must be explained, this section begins for that purpose.
And since that must be inquired into precisely through scripture (*āgama*), the scripture is presented here by means of a traditional narrative (*itihāsa*).—

the son of Aruṇa (Āruṇi), questioned him;

We lived in various regions,

We asked him, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am Kabandha by name,
and Ātharvaṇa, the descendant of Atharvan."
That Gāndharva said to Patañcala Kāpya and his disciples who were performers of sacrifices: "Do you know, O Kāpya, that thread? Do you know it?
What is that thread by which this world and this birth [are held together]?"
The world beyond, the future birth to be attained,
and all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— all these are strung together, woven like a garland on a thread, and supported by that upon which they depend; do you know what that thread is?
Being thus questioned, Kāpya replied: "I do not know that, O Blessed One;
I do not know that Sūtra, O Blessed One," speaking thus in a spirit of reverence.
Then the Gandharva spoke again to the teacher and to us: "Do you not know, O Kāpya, that Inner Controller?"
He is distinguished as the "Inner Controller" (antaryāmī)— he who, being within and internal to this world, the next world, and all beings, controls and governs them,
making them revolve like a wooden machine and causing each to perform its own appropriate function.
Thus addressed, Patañcala Kāpya replied, "I do not know him, O Blessed One," speaking while offering his respects.
Then the Gandharva spoke again;
the knowledge of both the *sūtra* and the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) contained within it is being praised: "Whosoever indeed, O Kāpya, should know that *sūtra*..."
One should know him as the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) contained within the Sūtra, and one should know him as the ruler of that very Sūtra—in the manner thus described.

For he is the knower of Brahman, the knower of the Supreme Self; he knows the worlds, such as Bhūr and the others, governed by the Inner Controller, and he knows the gods, such as Agni and the rest, who inhabit those worlds.
He knows the Vedas as being the source of all authority;
he knows the beings, beginning with Brahmā, as being held by the Thread (Sūtra) and governed by the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) residing within them;
and he knows himself as characterized by agency and enjoyership, likewise governed by that very same Inner Controller.
And he knows that the entire world is thus constituted.

When the Sūtra and the Antaryāmin-consciousness had been praised in this manner, Kāpya became desirous and appeared before him, as did we; and to us, who had appeared before him, the Gandharva spoke concerning the Sūtra and the Antaryāmin.

Therefore, having received the traditional teaching from the Gandharva, I know that Sūtra and that Antaryāmin. O Yājñavalkya, if you, while not knowing that Sūtra and that Antaryāmin, drive away the Brahman-cows— driving up the cows that belong to those who know Brahman— then your head shall clearly shatter, being consumed by my curse.

Thus addressed, Yājñavalkya said: "I know it, O Gautama"—referring to his lineage—"that thread which the Gandharva told you about, and that Inner Controller whom you learned from the Gandharva; I know that Inner Controller."
Thus addressed, Gautama replied: "If some common person were to say what you have said here—how so?
'I know, I know!'—boasting of himself, what would be the use of that roaring? Show the result through action."
"Speak as you know it. //1//
He said: "Vāyu, O Gautama, is indeed that thread.
By Vāyu, O Gautama, as by a thread, this world, the other world, and all beings are held together."
"Therefore, indeed, Gautama, they say of a dead man: 'His limbs have fallen apart.
For, Gautama, they are held together by the thread of wind.
"It is even so, Yājñavalkya."
"Tell me about the inner controller."
Yājñavalkya said:
"The worlds of Brahman are those in which [all things] are woven together and interwoven during the present time, just as the earth is woven upon the waters."
Since it must be stated that this "thread" (sūtra) is to be understood through scripture, another question is raised for that purpose;

therefore, to determine its nature, he says: "O Gautama, that thread is indeed air, and nothing else. By "air," one means that which is subtle like space and serves as the support for the earth and the other elements.

That which constitutes the seventeenfold subtle body (*liṅga*) of living beings, which is associated with the impressions of karma, and which exists as both a collective totality and as individual parts— of which the external manifestations are the seven groups of seven winds, like the waves of the ocean.
This very principle of air (*vāyavya-tattva*) is called the "thread" (*sūtra*).
For it is well known, O Gautama, that by the thread of air, this world, the other world, and all beings are strung together and held spread out. And there is a common worldly saying; how so?
Because wind is the thread and everything is held together by wind,
therefore, O Gautama, they say of a deceased person: "The limbs of this person have fallen apart," meaning they have become disintegrated.

"For when the thread is removed, whatever parts of jewels and such things were strung upon it would fall apart; therefore, this is logical: that the falling apart of the parts occurs upon the removal of the air. Thus, Gautama, they are held together by the thread of air"—with these words he concludes.
"It is even so, Yājñavalkya; you have correctly stated the thread."
When it was asked, "Now, tell us of that Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) who is contained within that very Sūtra and who governs it," he replied: //2//

He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, and who controls the earth from within— He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
He who dwells in the earth is the Inner Controller (antaryāmī).
To avoid the over-extension that "everyone" dwells in the earth, he specifies: "interior to the earth," meaning within it.

In this regard, it might be thought that the deity of the earth itself is the Inner Controller; therefore, he says: "That Inner Controller whom even the deity of the earth does not know, thinking, 'Someone else exists within me'—he whose body is the earth, and for whom the earth alone is the body, and nothing else—that [Inner Controller] is distinct from the body of the deity of the earth."
That very thing which has the body as its [substrate]—
the mention of the "body" being intended as an illustration—
and that which is the instrument of the earth.
For the activity of the Earth-deity is indeed impelled by her own karma; however, because that [karma] is absent in this case— since the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) is eternally liberated—
and because the Supreme Being has as his very nature the duty to act for the sake of others, whatever task or instrument belongs to the Supreme is itself his.
Not from itself;
as it has been said: "He whose body is the earth.
For the activity and cessation of the organs that perform the functions of the deities would occur through the necessary presence of the mere witness, the Lord.
This Lord, named Nārāyaṇa, who is such as this,
governs and restrains Pṛthivī, the deity of the earth, in her own activity.
Dwelling within as the inner one,
this is your self, yours.

And the phrase "of me and of all beings" is intended as an illustration; he who is the inner controller (antaryāmī) whom you have not asked about is immortal, meaning devoid of all the qualities of saṃsāra. //3//

In the sky,

This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
Other than this, everything is subject to suffering.

and he who is in speech,
and in the eye.
In the ear,
in the mind,
and in the skin.
In consciousness, in the intellect, in semen, and in procreation.

For what reason, then, do the highly fortunate deities of the earth and other elements not perceive the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), the Ruler of themselves, who dwells within their own hearts like a human being? To this he says: "He is unseen" (*adṛṣṭena*), meaning He has not become an object for the vision of anyone;
yet, because He Himself is present within the eye, He is the Seer (*draṣṭā*) whose very nature is seeing.
Likewise, "unheard" means not having entered the range of anyone's hearing;
yet, being Himself possessed of unimpaired power of hearing and present in all ears, He is the "Hearer.
Similarly, "unthought" means not having entered the sphere of mental volition.
For everyone indeed forms conceptual constructions based on what has been seen and heard;
he is the "seer" because he is not unseen, and the "unborn" for the same reason;
he is the "thinker" because he possesses the power of speech and thought, and because he is present within all minds.
Thus, being unperceived and not having entered the domain of determinate cognition— unlike form and so forth, or like pleasure and so forth—
it is itself the perceiver because its power of consciousness is undiminished and due to its proximity [to all things].
In this regard, it follows that there is one who is the controller and inner ruler (antaryāmī), distinct from those other perceivers whom "the earth does not know" and "whom all beings do not know."
To eliminate the suspicion that [the Self] might be something other than that, it is said:
"Not other than this," meaning there is no seer other than this Inner Controller;
likewise, there is no thinker other than this.
There is no other hearer than this; there is no other thinker than this; there is no other cognizer than this.
Because there is no other seer, hearer, thinker, or knower beyond this;
he who is the unseen seer, the unheard hearer, and so forth.
The Knower who is unknown, the Conscious One who is unconscious,

the Immortal who is devoid of all the phenomena of saṃsāra, and the ordainer of the distribution of the fruits of karma for all those in saṃsāra— this is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. Other than this Īśvara-Self, everything else is afflicted.
