The King of Videha, or a king of the Videhas—

meaning one whose son is fierce and who belongs to a lineage of heroes— having made his unstrung bow (one from which the string has been removed) strung again (having mounted the string upon it), [prepared] two arrows; by the word "arrow" (*bāṇa*), that piece of bamboo is meant which is joined to the tip of the shaft.

Since an arrow can exist even without a shaft, he specifies "two with shafts"—meaning two arrows equipped with shafts. Their further qualification is "piercing the enemy exceedingly," meaning causing intense pain to the foe.

"Taking them in hand, one should stand up" means one should show oneself nearby; in this very way, I have stood up near you with these two questions, which take the place of arrows. I have risen in your presence.
"Tell these two to me," [Yājñavalkya said]. If he is a knower of Brahman, the other should say: "Ask, Gārgī. //2//
She said: "Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two— the sky and the earth—
and that which they call the past, the present, and the future— across what is that woven, warp and woof?"

She said: "That which is above, beyond the upper shell of the cosmic egg; that which is below, beneath the earth, under the lower shell of the cosmic egg; and that which is between, in the middle of heaven and earth—that is, between the two shells of heaven and earth—and these very two, heaven and earth."
That which has been, that which is past;
that which is becoming, existing in its own activity in the present;
and that which will be, to be known by signs occurring at a time subsequent to the present—all this they declare and speak of according to tradition (āgama).

The meaning is that in which all that collection of duality becomes unified—that previously mentioned thing known as the *sūtra*—in what is it woven lengthwise and crosswise, like the element of earth in water? //3//

He said: "O Gārgī, that which is above heaven, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future— across all this,
[the Imperishable] is woven as warp and woof."
The other said: "O Gārgī, as for what you have said— that which they call the 'thread' (sūtra) above heaven and so forth— that thread is woven across and through space."

This manifested world, consisting of the nature of the Sūtras, exists within the unmanifested Ākāśa—like the element of earth in water—throughout all three times: during its origination, its persistence, and its dissolution. //4//
She said: "Homage be to you, Yājñavalkya, for you have explained this to me. Hold it for another. "Ask, Gārgī," he replied.
Again she said:
"Salutations to you," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the difficulty of answering her question;
for you have answered this question of mine by setting it aside through a qualification.

The reason for its being difficult to explain is this: the Sūtra itself is already incomprehensible and difficult to express for others; how much more so that in which [the world] is woven both lengthwise and crosswise?
Therefore, let there be homage to you;
"to the other," meaning to the second question, "hold fast"—that is, make yourself firm.
"Ask, Gārgī," said the other. //5//
She said: "Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two— the sky and the earth—
and that which they call the past, the present, and the future— across what is that woven, warp and woof?"
The rest has been explained.

She said, "What is above that, Yājñavalkya? and so forth; this question and its answer are stated again for the purpose of confirming the very meaning already expressed; no new or different matter whatsoever is being stated. //6//

He said: "O Gārgī, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future— all that is woven, warp and woof, upon space alone."
"In what, then, is space woven to and fro? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.7)
Having repeated everything exactly as stated by Gārgī, Yājñavalkya confirmed that very point previously mentioned: "In space alone [is it woven].
Gārgī said: "But in what, indeed, is space woven across and lengthwise?
Space itself, being beyond the three periods of time, is difficult to define.

Even more difficult than that is the syllable in which space is woven as warp and woof; because it is thus inexpressible, one does not comprehend it— this non-comprehension is called a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in the system of logicians.
Even if he were to state what is inexpressible,
it would still be the point of defeat known as *vipratipatti* (contradictory apprehension), for that is indeed a contradictory apprehension.
Since this is the speaking of that which is unspeakable, Gārgī considers this question difficult to answer.
Desiring to avoid both of those faults,
he said: "Gārgī, the Brahmins indeed declare that this Imperishable (akṣara) to be neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long."

It is not long, not red, not viscous, not shadowy, not dark, not airy, not ethereal, unattached, tasteless, odorless, without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind, without radiance, without breath, without mouth, without limbs— indeed, it is without interior and without exterior;
it does not eat anything at all.
No one at all eats that.
Yājñavalkya said: "This indeed is that which you asked: 'In what, then, is space woven like warp and woof? What is that?

It is the Imperishable (akṣara)—that which does not waste away (na kṣīyate) and does not perish (na kṣarati). Therefore it is called the Imperishable. O Gārgī, those Brahmins who know Brahman speak of it as the Imperishable. By this statement identifying it as Brahman, he avoids two faults: namely, that he might say something unspeakable, or that he might fail to provide a satisfactory answer. Thus he dispels these two defects.
When the question had been thus refuted, Gārgya’s reply is to be seen again: "Tell me, what is that syllable which the Brāhmaṇas declare?
Being thus addressed, he said: "It is not gross (*aprasthūlam*)," meaning it is other than the gross.
If that is so, then is it minute? It is not minute. Well then, let it be short; it is not short. If that is so, then let it be long.
Nor is it long or short;
thus, by these four negations of dimension, its quality as a substance is negated—
the meaning being that this syllable is not a substance.
Let it be, then, that redness is a quality,
and that which is other than that is non-red;
redness is the fiery quality.
Let it be, then, that it has viscidity; no, it does not have viscidity; let it be, then, that it is a shadow;
in any case, because it is indefinable.
There is something other than even shadow, which is non-shadow;
let it then be darkness, or rather, non-darkness; or let it then be wind.
If it were without air, then it would be space;
if it were not space, then let it be of the nature of attachment like lac;
if it were non-attached, then let it be taste.
"Let it be tasteless; likewise, let there be no smell; let there be no smell then. Now, as for the eye:
let it be eyeless—for indeed no instrument of seeing exists for it, therefore it is eyeless."
"He sees without eyes," according to the words of the mantra; likewise, "he hears without ears."
Let it be, then, that it is without speech and likewise without mind; likewise, it is without luster— meaning that luster does not exist in it, thus it is "without luster" (atejaska).
For it possesses no heat such as the light of fire and the like;
"without breath"—by this, the internal vital air (vāyu) is negated; "without a mouth"—then the mouth is its door, and thus it is "mouthless."
That by which something is measured is a measure (*mātra*); that which is not a measure (*amātra*) does not have the form of a measure, for nothing at all is measured by it.
Let it be, then, like a void (*chidra*).
There is no interval for it;
therefore, it might exist externally, yet it is not external. Let it then be the eater; yet it does not eat anything at all.
In that case, it would be edible for someone,
yet no one eats it;
the meaning is that it is devoid of all specific qualities.
For that which is indeed one without a second—by what could it be distinguished from what?
Although the existence of the Imperishable has been established by the Śruti through the effort of negating numerous qualifications,
nevertheless, with regard to the understanding of worldly people, a doubt may still arise;
therefore, he sets forth inference as a means of knowledge to establish its existence:
"By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart;
by the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart."
"Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the moments, the muhūrtas, the days and nights, the half-months, the months, the seasons, and the years stand held apart.
Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, some rivers flow eastward from the white mountains, and others flow westward, or toward whichever direction they may be.
Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, humans praise the sacrificer; the gods depend upon the oblation-ladle, and the ancestors depend upon the ancestral offering."
Or, O Gārgī, by the command of the Imperishable, humans praise those who give, and the gods praise the sacrificer.
The ancestors are dependent upon the wooden ladle. // 9 //
"Of this very syllable"—
that which has been understood as the syllable, the innermost of all, the Brahman that is immediate and direct,
the Self that transcends the attributes of hunger and so forth— of that [is it said].

Or rather, under the governance of this Imperishable— just as a kingdom remains intact and orderly under the governance of a king— even so, O Gārgī, under the governance of this Imperishable, the sun and the moon, which serve as the lamps of the world for day and night,
were created by that Governor who possesses the knowledge of the purposes of the world to be accomplished through them.
They must be common to all living beings and beneficial to their illumination, like an ordinary worldly lamp.

Therefore, there exists that by which the two Lords are sustained, established as independent, created, and remain so; they proceed through regulated rise and setting, increase and decrease, according to specific place, time, and cause.
Thus, there certainly exists for these two an imperishable Ruler.

It is like the maker, the holder, and the sustainer of a lamp. Or rather, O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable, heaven and earth— though they possess parts and are thus subject to bursting, though they are heavy and thus subject to falling, and though they are joined and thus subject to separation— remain so because they are presided over by conscious deities endowed with self-conceit.
Even in the independent [world], these two remain supported and held apart by the governance of this Imperishable;
for this Imperishable is the bridge of all order and the upholder of all boundaries;
therefore, heaven and earth do not overstep the governance of this Imperishable.
Therefore, the existence of this Imperishable is established, for that is its infallible mark:
that heaven and earth remain held in their place.
Without a conscious Ruler who is not subject to transmigratory existence, this would not be possible.
From the wording of the mantra: "By whom the fierce heaven and the earth were seen"; and [from the Śruti]:

"O Gārgī, under the command of this Imperishable One, these divisions of time—moments, hours, and so forth—are the reckoners of everything born, past, future, and present; just as in the world a calculator appointed by a master [reckons] all income and expenditure."
And just as one who is vigilant counts [the time],
so too is the Lord the controller of these divisions of time.
Likewise, rivers that flow forward— meaning those that move toward the eastern direction— flow and stream forth from the white mountains, such as the Himavat and others.

Just as the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, having been set in motion from the mountains and peaks, continue to flow in their fixed course even though they might otherwise have been capable of flowing differently—
this is a sign of a Ruler.
The other rivers, such as the Sindhu and others, flow toward the western direction; and those which have set out toward whichever direction they may be, do not deviate from it—
this is a sign.
Furthermore, even when one gives gold and other gifts, causing oneself distress, people who understand the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) praise that act;
in that regard, both that which is given and those who give it [are to be praised].
And as for those who accept [these gifts],
their meeting and dissolution right here in this world are seen immediately; however, the subsequent meeting in the hereafter is unseen.

Nevertheless, seeing that those who give are joined with the fruit of their gift, human beings praise [the giver] because they understand the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa); and that [result] would not exist if there were no ordainer who joins one with the fruit of action and who knows the distribution of the fruits of the agent's actions,
since the act of giving perishes perceptibly.
Therefore, there exists one who connects the donors with the fruit.

If it is argued that this [connector] is a "novelty" (apūrva), that is not so, because no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) can be established for its existence. If it is further argued that this applies to the praiser as well...

No, because the purport of the scripture is already established; we have stated that the scripture has reality as its ultimate object. Furthermore, there would be no need for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) in the postulation of the *apūrva*.
[The opponent's position] is refuted because [the desired result] arises in a different manner;
for it is observed that the fruit of service is obtained from the one being served,
and because service is an action.

And because of that similarity, the attainment of results from the Lord and other objects of service through speech, gifts, oblations, and so forth, is logically established; for when the assumption of the attainment of results can be justified without abandoning the observed capacity of ritual action, it is not right to abandon that observed capacity of ritual action.
This is also because it would involve an excessive multiplication of assumptions (*kalpanādhikya*).
Is the Lord the cause, or is it the *apūrva* (unseen potency)?
In that regard, the attainment of a fruit from that which is to be served is observed to be the inherent nature of action (*kriyā*), but not from an *apūrva*;
nor is an *apūrva* ever observed.

In that case, one must postulate a novel, unseen entity (apūrva-adṛṣṭa), as well as its capacity to bestow the fruit, and once that capacity exists, the act of giving itself becomes redundant. Here, however, one need only postulate the mere existence of the Lord, who is the object of service.
But the capacity to bestow a fruit and the state of being a giver [belong to the Lord],
because it is observed that the attainment of fruits comes from one who is served;
and inference has also been shown in such passages as, "Heaven and earth stand held apart."
And likewise, although the gods are lords, they have followed after the sacrificer for the sake of their livelihood,
with the purpose of subsisting on the sacrificial charu, puroḍāśa, and so forth;
for even though they are capable of living otherwise, they remain by resorting to this wretched and miserable mode of existence.
And that [result] would come from the instruction of the instructor.
Likewise, the ancestors also, for that purpose, are "connected with" (anvāyattāḥ)—meaning following along with—the *darvī* and the *darvīhoma*;
everything else is the same. //9//
For this reason as well, that Imperishable exists, because it is certain that the occurrence of saṃsāra follows from ignorance of it;
moreover, it must exist, since its cessation results from the knowledge of it.
Because it is logically established.
If it is argued that its cessation must occur through action alone, we say no—
BrhUp 3.8.10.
"Or, Gārgī, whoever in this world offers oblations, sacrifices, or performs austerities for many thousands of years without knowing this syllable—his [merit] becomes merely finite.
Or, Gārgī, whoever departs from this world without knowing this syllable, he is pitiable.
But he, Gārgī, who departs from this world having known this syllable, he is a true Brahmin."
"O Gārgī, whoever in this world offers oblations, performs sacrifices, or practices austerities without knowing this Imperishable— even if it be for many thousands of years—
his fruit is indeed finite; at the end of the enjoyment of that fruit, his works are simply exhausted."
Moreover, that imperishable Being which, when known, brings about the transcendence of wretchedness and the cessation of saṃsāra—

that very Being, through whose absence the agent of action becomes miserable, merely an enjoyer of the fruits of his deeds, and wanders in saṃsāra mounted upon the continuous cycle of birth and death—
exists as the ruler.
This is what is being said: "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is miserable, like a slave bought for a price;
but he, O Gārgī, who departs from this world having known this Imperishable, is a true Brāhmaṇa. (10)
Since fire possesses the qualities of burning and illuminating as its inherent nature, one might think that the quality of being a ruler belongs only to something insentient; therefore, he says:
"Now, this very syllable, O Gārgī, is unseen but the seer, unheard but the hearer, unthought but the thinker, unperceived but the perceiver. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11)
There is no seer other than this; there is no hearer other than this; there is no thinker other than this.
There is no other knower than this.
Indeed, O Gārgī, in this very Imperishable, space is woven like warp and woof.
Now, this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, is unseen; it has not been seen by anyone because it is not an object [of perception], yet it is itself the seer because its nature is vision.
Likewise, it is unheard, because it is not an object of the sense of hearing.
It is itself the hearer because its nature is hearing;
likewise, it is itself the thinker because the mind is not its object and its nature is the intellect of the thinker.
Likewise, it is not known by another because it is not an object of the intellect (*buddhi*);
it is itself the knower because its very nature is consciousness.
Furthermore, there is nothing other than this Imperishable—there exists no other seer who is the agent of the act of seeing.
This very syllable is the agent of the act of seeing everywhere;
likewise, there is no other hearer than this,
for that same syllable is the hearer everywhere.
There is no other thinker than this;
that very Imperishable is the thinker everywhere through every door of the mind.
There is no other knower than this, the agent of the act of knowing.
That very Imperishable (akṣara) is the agent of the functions of cognition and action through the door of all the intellects; it is not the insentient Pradhāna or anything else.
For it is said: "In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven like warp and woof."
That which is Brahman— directly perceptible and not hidden—
that Self which is within all, transcending the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and so forth,
and in which space is woven like warp and woof.
This is the supreme goal,
this is the supreme attainment,
this is the supreme Brahman.
This is the truth of the truth of everything from earth up to space. //11//
She said: "Venerable Brahmins, you should consider yourselves fortunate enough that you may be released from us by a mere salutation;
for indeed, no one shall ever defeat you in this debate on Brahman."
Thereupon, Vācaknavī ceased questioning.
She said: "O venerable Brahmins, listen to my words; you should hold that very thing in high esteem. What is it?
That by which you may be released from this Yājñavalkya—meaning, having offered him salutation, you should hold that very act in high esteem."
His victory is not even to be hoped for in thought, much less in action; why?
Because, indeed, among you there is never at any time anyone who can defeat this Yājñavalkya in a debate concerning Brahman.
"I have already declared that if he answers these two questions for me, he will not be my conqueror;
even now, this remains my firm conviction— that there exists no one equal to me in this theological debate."
Thereupon Vācaknavī indeed ceased [questioning].
In this Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa, it is stated: "Him whom the earth does not know, and whom all beings do not know."

Regarding that Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) whom they do not know, and that Imperishable (Akṣara) which they do not know—which has been described as the element of consciousness and so forth for all beings by virtue of being the seer and the non-agent—what is the distinction between these two, or what is their commonality?
On this point, some explain: of the Supreme Brahman, who is like the great ocean and whose nature is immovability, the state of slight movement is the Inner Controller;
the state of extreme movement is the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña).
He who does not know that Inner Controller (antaryāmin);
likewise, others postulate five states,
while others say that there are eight states of Brahman.
Some say that these are the powers (śakti) of the Imperishable (akṣara), and that the Imperishable possesses infinite powers;
others, however, say that they are the transformations (vikāra) of the Imperishable.
To begin with, both states and powers are not possible for the Imperishable (akṣara),
because of the scriptural teaching that it transcends the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and so forth.
For it is not possible for one and the same thing to simultaneously possess both the transcendence of hunger and the like, and the possession of states characterized by hunger and the like.
Likewise, [the arguments for] its possessing power and its being subject to modification or having parts have already been shown to be fallacious in the fourth chapter.
Therefore, all these conceptual constructions are unreal.
What, then, is their difference?
We say it is caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi);
in themselves, there is neither difference nor non-difference among them.
Because its essential nature is the single flavor of the mass of pure consciousness, like a solid block of rock salt;

and because of the Śruti texts: "Without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior," and "This Self is Brahman," as well as in the Atharva Veda: "For He is indeed unborn, both within and without."

Therefore, because the self (ātman) is without limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), is indefinable (nirupākhya), devoid of distinctions (nirviśeṣa), and unitary (eka), it is designated as "not this, not this" (neti neti).

When the self is characterized by the limiting adjuncts of ignorance (avidyā), desire (kāma), and action (karman), consisting of the body and the organs, it is called the transmigrating individual soul (jīva).
When the self is characterized by the limiting adjunct of the power of eternal and unsurpassed knowledge, it is called the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) or the Lord (īśvara).
That very [Self], when free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*), alone, pure, and by its own nature, is called the Imperishable (*akṣara*) and the Supreme (*para*).

Likewise, when qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as Hiraṇyagarbha, the Undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*), the deities, the species, the physical body, humans, animals, ghosts, and so forth—which are effects and instruments—it becomes designated by those names and takes on those forms.
Thus it has been explained: "It moves; it does not move."

Thus, scriptural passages such as "This is your Self," "This is the inner Self of all beings," "He is hidden in all beings," "That thou art," "I alone am all this," "The Self alone is all this," and "There is no other seer but He" are not contradicted;
these scriptures do not apply under any other conceptual framework.
Therefore, their distinction is due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and not otherwise;
for in all the Upaniṣads there is the restrictive determination: "One only, without a second. //12//
Thus ends the eighth section, the Akṣara-Brāhmaṇa, of the third chapter.
Then Vidagdha Śākalya questioned him.

Having explained how the earth and the other elements—arranged in a sequence of increasing subtlety—are woven like warp and woof, each preceding one within each succeeding one, he revealed the Brahman that is the innermost of all; and [he further explained] that Brahman in relation to the realm of the manifest, within the various threads of the cosmic thread (*sūtra*).
The state of being a controller has already been mentioned; it is said that in the realm of the manifested, the indicative mark (liṅga) is more manifest.

Since that very Brahman must be understood as directly perceptible through the means of the contraction and expansion of the various distinctions among the deities who are to be controlled, for this purpose the Śākalya-Brāhmaṇa is commenced. — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.1.

Then Vidagdha Śākalya questioned him: "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? He answered with this very *nivid*: as many as are mentioned in the *nivid* of the Vaiśvadeva hymn—"Three hundred and three, and three thousand and three."
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya?
"Thirty-three," he replied.
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "Six," he replied.
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "Three," he replied.
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "Two," he replied.
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "One and a half," he replied.
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "One," he replied.
"Om," he said.
"Which are those three and three hundred, and three and three thousand? 3.9.1.
Then Śākalya, the descendant of Śakala known by the name Vidagdha, questioned him: "How many gods are there, O Yājñavalkya?
That Yājñavalkya, it is said—
He established the number by means of this very *nivid* which is about to be mentioned—the very number that Śākalya had asked about.
"As many" (*yāvantaḥ*) means however many in number the gods are of the *vaiśvadeva* recitation; a *nivid* consists of mantra-words that express the number of deities.
Certain verses are recited during the Vaiśvadeva Śastra, and these are designated as *nivid*.

As many deities as are heard mentioned in that *nivid*, so many deities [are present]. What, then, is that *nivid*? Those *nivid* words are demonstrated: "Three hundred and three," meaning three hundred and three deities.
"Three hundred and three gods;
and again, likewise, three and three thousand—there are this many gods," said Śākalya; "So be it," he replied.
Thus, this middle number of theirs has been correctly understood;
then he asks again regarding the number of those same gods in their contracted state: "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya?"—the answer is "Thirty-three."
Three, two, one and a half, and one.

Having asked about the number of deities regarding their contraction and expansion, he asks again about the nature of those who are numbered: "Which are those three and three hundred, and three and three thousand? (1)
He said:
"These are merely their manifestations;
there are indeed only thirty-three gods."
"What are those thirty-three?
"The eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, and the twelve Ādityas—those are thirty-one; and Indra and Prajāpati make up the thirty-three. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.2)
The other said: "These are the greatnesses, the manifestations—namely, these 'three and three hundred' and so forth belonging to these thirty-three gods;
but in ultimate reality, there are indeed only thirty-three gods."
Which are those thirty-three? It is said: the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, and the twelve Ādityas—these make thirty-one;
Indra and Prajāpati are the thirty-second and thirty-third, completing the number thirty-three. //2//
"Which are the Vasus?
"Fire, earth, wind, intermediate space, sun, sky, moon, and stars— these are the Vasus."
For in them all this wealth (vasu) is placed; therefore they are called the Vasus.
"Which are the Vasus?"—thus their individual nature is asked.

"Agni and the Earth," etc.—these, beginning with Agni and ending with the stars, are the Vasus. They cause this entire world to dwell (*vasayanti*) and they themselves dwell (*vasanti*), because they transform into the form of the aggregate of effects and instruments (the body and organs) as the locus for the fruits of the actions of living beings.
Because they dwell (vasanti) there, therefore they are called the Vasus. //3//
"Which are the Rudras?
"These ten vital breaths in a person, with the self as the eleventh."
When they depart from this mortal body, they cause one to weep;
because they cause one to weep (rodayanti), they are therefore called Rudras.

"Who are the Rudras? "These ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person—the five organs of action and the five organs of perception—and the self (*ātman*), the mind (*manas*), as the eleventh, which completes the group of eleven; when these vital breaths depart from this mortal body at the exhaustion of the living beings' enjoyment of the fruits of their karma, they then cause one to weep."
They are his relatives.
Because they cause him to weep there, they are therefore called Rudras. //4//
"Which are the Ādityas?
"The twelve months of the year— these are the Ādityas."
For these, taking all this [world] with them, depart; because they depart taking all this with them, they are called Ādityas.
"Which are the Ādityas? [The answer is:
The twelve months are well known as the constituent parts of time, the year; these are the Ādityas. How so?

For since these, revolving again and again, take up and seize the lifespans and the fruits of karma of living beings, and thus they go—that is, they proceed—taking all this, therefore they are called Ādityas. //5//
"Who is Indra? Who is Prajāpati? "The thunderclap is indeed Indra; the sacrifice is Prajāpati."
"What is thunder? "It is lightning.
"What is sacrifice?"
"Animals," [he said]. BrhUp 3.9.6.
"Who is Indra? Who is Prajāpati? "Indra is indeed the thunder, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice.
"What is the thunder? "It is the lightning bolt."
The thunderbolt is the vajra, which is vigor and strength;
that which causes living beings to perish is Indra, for that is indeed the deed of Indra.
"What is the sacrifice? "It is the sacrificial animals. For sacrificial animals are the means for accomplishing the sacrifice;
because the sacrifice is formless and because it relies upon the sacrificial animals as its means, the sacrificial animals are called the sacrifice. //6//
"Which are the six?
"Fire and earth, wind and the intermediate space, the sun and the sky— these are the six."
For these six indeed constitute this entire universe.
"Which are the six?
These very ones previously mentioned as the Vasus, beginning with Agni and the rest, become six when excluding the moon and the stars—thus characterized by the number six.
All that was stated previously, beginning with the thirty-three, constitutes this [total].
These are indeed six; for the entire expansion beginning with Vasu is included within these very six—this is the meaning. //7//
"Which are those three gods? "These very three worlds."
"For within these two, all these gods are contained.
"Which are those two gods? "Food and breath alone."
"What is the one and a half?
"This wind that blows. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.8)
"Which are those three gods?
"These very three worlds"— having unified the earth and fire as one god, and having unified the intermediate space and wind as the third— these indeed are the three gods.
For in these three gods all gods are included; therefore, there are only these three gods—this is the position of certain etymologists (nairuktas).
Which are those two gods? Food and breath—these are the two gods.
The inclusion of all those mentioned is within these two. Which one is the Adhyarha? It is this wind that blows. (8)
Regarding this,
they say: "Since this [wind] blows as if it were only one,
how then is it 'one and a half'?"
Because all this was contained within him, he is called "Adhyardha" (the One-and-a-Half).
"Which is the one god? "Prāṇa," he replied.
They call that Brahman "Tyat" (That).
Regarding this, they raise an objection: "Since this wind blows as if it were only one, being indeed just one, how then can it be 'one and a half' (adhyardha)?
Because in this [wind], all this has grown full (adhyārdhnot)—while this wind exists, all this has grown full (adhyārdhnot), that is, it has attained prosperity."
Therefore, it is called "the one and a half. Which is that one deity?
It is *prāṇa*. That *prāṇa* is Brahman; because it consists of all the deities, it is the Great Brahman (*mahad brahma*).
Therefore, they call that Brahman "Tyat"—they designate that Brahman with the word "Tyat," which is an indirect (parokṣa) expression.
This constitutes both the unity and the diversity of the gods:
the inclusion of the infinite gods within those distinguished by specific numerical limits.
Among those as well, from the Thirty-three and so forth, in each successive stage down to a single breath (*prāṇa*),
the entire expansion reckoned as infinite belongs to that very single breath.
Thus, the one and the infinite, distinguished by intermediate numbers, is indeed the breath alone.
And in that regard, there is a distinction in the names, forms, functions, qualities, and powers of each individual deity, due to the difference in their respective offices. //9//
Now, the eightfold division of that very Prāṇa-Brahman is taught again:
"He whose abode is the earth, whose world is fire, whose light is the mind— he who would know that Person as the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower."
"Yājñavalkya, do you indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak?
That very person who is embodied—that is he.
Speak, Śākalya; who is his deity?"
"It is the immortal," he said. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.9.10.
The deity whose abode is the earth— that is, whose support is the earth— and whose world is fire— where "world" (*loka*) means that by which one sees, meaning one sees by means of fire.
"Manojyotiḥ": he who performs the functions of volition, conceptualization, and so forth by means of the light of the mind (manasā jyotiṣā) is "manojyotiḥ.

The meaning is that this deity possesses a body of earth, has fire as his organ of vision, is the conceiver through the mind, identifies with the earth, and is endowed with the aggregate of causes and effects (the body and its instruments).

Whoever should thus know— that is, discern— that distinguished Person as the supreme resort (*parāyaṇa*), the ultimate support, of the entire self consisting of the aggregate of effects and instruments belonging to the internal self;

[as] the supreme resort of that which is born of the mother— consisting of skin, flesh, and blood, standing in the place of the field— for that which is born of the father— consisting of bone, marrow, and semen, standing in the place of the seed— and also for the self consisting of the instruments.
"He indeed would be a knower"—
the intention is that he who knows this thus would indeed be a wise knower.
"O Yājñavalkya, you, while not knowing him at all, are merely conceited as a scholar"— this is the intended meaning.
"If you have attained such proficiency in that knowledge, then I truly know that Person about whom you speak—that ultimate resort of every self.
In this regard, Śākalya’s reply is to be considered: "If you know that Person..."
Tell me, what is his specific qualification?
He is this very one who is "bodily" (śārīra)—meaning, he exists within the body that consists of the earthly portion; that is to say, he is of the nature of the three sheaths born of the mother.
He is that very one.
O Śākalya, as for the deity you have questioned,
what further qualification could there be to be stated regarding him?
"Tell that! Ask that!"—this is the meaning. O Śākalya!
Thus provoked, overcome by indignation, he spoke like an elephant struck by a goad: "What is the deity of that body of the god?
For in this context, it is intended that the deity of something is that from which it is produced.
"It is nectar," he said.
"Nectar" refers to that essence of the food consumed which is the cause for the production of the blood derived from the mother;
therefore, from the essence of food, blood is produced and resides in the woman.
And thereafter, the body consists of blood and serves as the substratum for the seed;
the rest is the same. //10//

"Desire alone is his abode, the heart is his world, and the mind is his light— the person who knows that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. "Yājñavalkya, I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak."
"That person who consists of desire is this very one. Tell me, Śākalya, what is his deity? "Women," he said.
"Desire alone is his abode"—desire being the longing for sexual union with women; the meaning is that desire is his body.
"The heart is his world"—he sees by means of the heart, that is, by means of the intellect (*buddhi*).
This very person who consists of desire (*kāmamaya*) even with respect to the internal self is indeed composed of desire.
"What is his deity? he asked. "Women," he replied; for from women the manifestation of desire is kindled. //11//

"Only he who knows that person whose abode is forms, whose world is the eye, whose light is the mind, and who is the ultimate resort of every self— he indeed would be a knower. 'Yājñavalkya, I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak.'"
"That person who is there in the sun, he is this very one. Tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity?
"Truth," he said.
"Form alone is its abode.
Forms are white, black, and so forth.
That very person who is in the sun—the person in the sun being the most distinguished effect of all forms—what is his deity?
"It is *satyā*," he said. "By *satyā*, the eye is meant;
for from the eye as the internal self (*adhyātma*) is produced the sun as the external deity (*adhidaivata*). //12//

"He whose abode is space, whose world is hearing, and whose light is the mind— he who would know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. "Yājñavalkya, I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak."
"That very person who is heard and perceived by hearing, he is this one.
Speak, Śākalya! Who is his deity? "The quarters," he said.

"Of whom space itself is the abode, who is this one who exists as the ear— the auditory faculty— and who specifically manifests at the time of hearing, being thus called *prātiśrutka* (the one related to sound)—
what deity is he?"
"The quarters," he said;
"for from the quarters this internal [self] is produced. //13//

"He whose abode is darkness, whose world is the heart, whose light is the mind— verily, he who would know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. "Yājñavalkya, I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak."
"That person who consists of shadow—this is he.
Tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? "Death," he said.
"Darkness indeed is his abode": here, "darkness" refers to the perpetual gloom of Śarva;
with respect to the self, it is the person consisting of shadow, that is, consisting of ignorance.
"What is its deity?
"Death," he said. Death, too, is the deity that is the cause of its production. //14//

"Whoever knows that person whose abode is forms, whose world is the heart, whose light is the mind, and who is the ultimate resort of every self— he indeed would be a knower. 'Yājñavalkya, I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak.'"
"The person who is here in the mirror is this very one.
Tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity?
"Truth," he said.
"Form itself is its abode.
In the previous [section], forms were mentioned as being common to all; here, however, specific forms that serve as illuminators are taken.
"What deity is there for the specific locus of the form-sphere (*rūpāyatana*)—namely, the mirror and so forth which serve as the substratum for the reflection? "The vital breath (*asu*," he said.
"The manifestation of that person called the reflection arises from *asu*, the vital breath. (15)

"Water indeed is his abode, the heart is his world, and the mind is his light— the person who would know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. "Yājñavalkya, I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak."
"That person who is here in the waters, he is this very one. Tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity?
"Varuṇa," he said.
"Water indeed is his abode.
All common waters are his abode; that is, he has a specific residence within the waters found in reservoirs such as ponds, wells, and tanks.
What is his deity?
"Varuṇa"; from Varuṇa comes the aggregate-former, which is the waters themselves—the cause of the production of water and so forth—within the self. //16//

"Seer Bṛhaspati, he who knows that person whose abode is semen, whose world is the heart, whose light is the mind, and who is the ultimate resort of every self— he indeed would be a knower. Yājñavalkya, I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak."
"That person who consists of sons—this is he.
Tell me, Śākalya, what is his deity? "Prajāpati," he replied.
"Seminal fluid itself is its abode"—
this refers to that which consists of the son, which is a specific abode of seminal fluid.
And as for the "son," the bones, marrow, and semen are produced from the father.
"Who is its deity? "Prajāpati," he replied.
Prajāpati is called the Father.
For the birth of a son indeed proceeds from the father. //17//

Each individual deity, having divided itself threefold by way of the distinction between the eightfold [deities], the worlds, and the person, remains established as a mere variety of vital breaths (*prāṇa*) for the purpose of meditation. Now, in order to conclude the teaching on the Self as divided fivefold according to the divisions of the directions,
Yājñavalkya spoke to Śākalya— who had become silent— as if possessing him with a spell:
"Śākalya," said Yājñavalkya,
"have these Brahmins indeed made you their charcoal-burner?"
"O Śākalya," Yājñavalkya said,
"the word *svid* is used here in the sense of inquiry;
surely these Brahmins..."

"Aṅgārāvakṣaṇa" refers to that pair of tongs or similar instrument in which the coals are extinguished; the meaning is this: "At that time, the Brahmins surely made you such [an instrument], yet you do not perceive yourself being burned by me. //18//
"Yājñavalkya," Śākalya said,
"since you have out-talked the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas, what Brahman do you know?"
"He knows the quarters together with their deities and foundations"—this refers to the fact that he knows the quarters together with their deities and foundations. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.19)

"Yājñavalkya," said Śākalya, "since you have spoken disparagingly of these Kurupañcāla Brahmins— you have overstepped them when they themselves, out of fear, made you carry their embers— how is it that, knowing Brahman,
you thus insult the Brahmins?"
Yājñavalkya said: "This much, indeed, is my knowledge of Brahman. What is it? I know the quarters; that is, I possess knowledge concerning the quarters.
And that is not merely the quarters alone."
"Together with the gods," meaning along with the deities who preside over the directions; furthermore, "together with their foundations," meaning along with the bases upon which they stand.
The other replied: "If you know the directions together with the gods..."
"Along with their foundations," this means if you have asserted that consciousness possesses its fruit. //19//
"Which deity are you in this eastern direction?
"The sun-deity," he replied.
"On what is that sun established?
"On the eyes. "But on what are the eyes established?"
Regarding the phrase "in forms":
for one sees forms with the eye;
[he asks], "In what, then, are forms established?"
"It is the heart," he said.
"For by the heart one knows forms;
for in the heart alone forms are established."
"Even so, Yājñavalkya. "Even so, Maitreyī. "This is indeed so, Yājñavalkya. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.20.
"Whose deity are you? "Whose deity is this [person] of yours who has become the quarters?

For Yājñavalkya had conceived of the heart—the Self—as divided fivefold among the quarters, having identified the entire world as the Self by means of that [heart] which has become the essence of the quarters.
"I am the self of the quarters," thus established, facing the east—because of the mention of his standing firm—he asks him just as Yājñavalkya had proposed: "What deity are you in this quarter?
For in every instance in the Veda, whichever deity one worships, [that deity is the one to whom the question is directed].
"Having become that very thing here, one attains each respective state"; and thus it will be said later: "Having become a god, one goes to the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.2).
In this eastern direction, which deity presides over you, whose self is the quarters?
"By which deity have you been endowed with this form?"—this is the meaning.
The other replied: "The deity is Āditya.
"In the eastern direction, Āditya is my deity."

Thus, I am the deity of the sun. It has been stated that "together with the gods," but it must now be said "together with their foundations. He asks: "In what is that sun established? [The answer is: "In the eye."

Regarding the internal [self], there are scriptural declarations in the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas* stating that the sun is produced from the eye, such as: "From the eye the sun was born" (*Yajurveda* 31.12) and "From the eye the sun" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 1.4), among others.
For indeed, the effect is established within its cause.
"On what is the eye established? "On forms. For the eye, which consists of form, is employed for the apprehension of forms;

indeed, by whatever forms it is employed, the eye is undertaken for the sake of grasping its own self, and thus, together with the eastern direction and all things situated therein, it is established upon forms.
"The eastern direction together with the eye consists of all forms;
and upon what, then, are those forms established? "Upon the heart," he said.
Forms are originated from the heart;
for the heart has transformed itself into the aspect of form,
since it is by means of the heart that all the world cognizes forms.
The term "heart" (*hṛdayam*) is a designation made by unifying the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*);
therefore, it is indeed in the heart that forms are established,
for it is through the heart that the recollection of forms— which exist in the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)— occurs.
Therefore, the meaning is that forms are established in the heart.
"It is exactly so, Yājñavalkya. //20//
"Which deity are you in this southern quarter?
"Yama is my deity."
"On what is that Yama established? "On sacrifice.
"But on what is sacrifice established?"
"Regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*):
upon what, then, is the sacrificial fee established? "Upon faith (*śraddhā*)."
"For when one has faith, then one gives a sacrificial gift;
for it is upon faith that the sacrificial gift is established.
"But upon what is faith established?"
"It is the heart," he said. "For by the heart one has faith;
indeed, it is in the heart that faith is established."
"Even so it is, Yājñavalkya. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.21.
"Which deity are you in this southern direction?"—as before.
"In the southern direction, which is the deity there? "The deity Yama."
Yama is the deity for me who have become the southern direction.
In what is that Yama established?
He is established in sacrifice—that is, together with the direction, Yama is established in the cause that is sacrifice.

How, then, is Yama the effect of the sacrifice? It is explained as follows: the sacrifice performed by the officiating priests is purchased back from them by the sacrificer with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); by means of that sacrifice, he conquers the southern direction together with Yama.
Thus, because Yama is the effect [of the sacrifice], he is established in the sacrifice along with the southern direction and the sacrificial fee.
"On what is the sacrifice established? "On the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). For by means of the sacrificial fee it is purchased; therefore, the sacrifice has the sacrificial fee as its function.
"On what is the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) established?
"On faith (śraddhā)," he replied. Faith is the desire to give, accompanied by a sense of conviction and devotion.
How is the sacrificial gift established upon that?
For when one has faith, then one gives a sacrificial gift; one does not give a sacrificial gift without faith.
Therefore, it is in faith indeed that the sacrificial gift is established.
"On what is faith established? "On the heart," he said, "for faith is a function of the heart; it is by means of the heart that one knows faith."
And a function is established upon that which possesses the function;
therefore, faith is indeed established in the heart.
"It is even so, Yājñavalkya. //21//
"Which deity are you in this western quarter?
"Varuṇa is my deity," he replied.
"On what is that Varuṇa established?
"In the waters. "On what, then, are the waters established?"
"Regarding semen:
upon what is semen established?
"Upon the heart."
Therefore they say that what is born is a worthy likeness, as if it had glided out from the heart, as if it were fashioned from the heart;
for indeed, the seed is established in the heart.
"It is even so, Yājñavalkya."
"Whose deity are you in this western direction?
"Varuṇa is my presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) in that direction.
"In what is that Varuṇa established?"
"In the waters"—for Varuṇa's function is indeed in the waters, according to the Vedic revelation: "The waters are faith; from faith he created Varuṇa.
In what, then, are the waters established?
Regarding "semen": for according to the Vedic scripture, "From semen indeed were the waters created.
In what is semen established?
In the heart—for semen is the effect of the heart.
Desire is the activity of the heart; for from the heart of one who desires, semen flows forth.

Therefore, people in the world say that a son born who is well-formed and corresponding [to his father] has emerged from the heart of this father as if asleep, or has been fashioned from the heart, just as an earring is fashioned from gold.
"Therefore, semen is indeed established in the heart.
"It is just so, Yājñavalkya. //22//
"Which deity are you in this northern direction?
"The Moon is my deity," he replied.
"On what is that Soma established?
"On consecration. "But on what is consecration established?"
"Truth. Therefore, they say to one who has been consecrated, "Speak the truth," for the consecration is established in truth alone.
"On what, then, is truth established?
"On the heart," he said,
"for it is by means of the heart that one knows truth."
"For truth is indeed established in the heart.
"It is just so, Yājñavalkya."
"Which deity are you in this northern direction?
"The Soma deity."—here, the plant *soma* and the deity *Soma* are designated by identifying them as one.
"In what is that Soma established?"

Regarding the phrase "in initiation" (dīkṣāyām): for it is the initiated sacrificer who purchases the Soma; having sacrificed with the purchased Soma, the possessor of knowledge proceeds toward the northern direction, which is the auspicious quarter presided over by the deity Soma.
But in what is initiation established?
"It is truth. How so?
Because initiation is established in truth, for that reason they say to one who has been initiated: "Speak the truth."
"Lest there be a failure in the cause, lest there be a failure in the effect—
for indeed, the consecration is established upon truth? "In the heart," he replied.
"For one knows truth through the heart; therefore, truth is established in the heart alone. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya. //23//
"Which deity are you in this fixed quarter?
"Agni is my deity," he replied.
"On what is that fire established?
"On speech.
"But on what is speech established?"
"In the heart. "In what, then, is the heart established? Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.24.
"Which deity are you in this direction?
Because it abounds in light for those dwelling all around Meru, the upward direction is called "the Fixed" (dhruvā).
"Agni is its deity"—for indeed, there is an abundance of light in the upward direction.
And fire is light.
Upon what is that fire established? "Upon speech.
Upon what is speech established? "Upon the heart."
In this regard, Yājñavalkya, with his heart extended toward all directions, has fully realized all the directions as his own self.

For that Yājñavalkya—who consists of name, form, and action—the directions, together with their deities and foundations, have become his very self. Whatever is his form, that, along with the eastern direction, has become his heart.

That which is mere action— characterized by the procreation of sons, accompanied by vehicles, and together with the presiding deities of the foam and the deities of the southern, western, and northern directions whose nature consists of the fruits of action— all this, along with the fixed direction (the zenith) as the heart itself, enters the heart alone through the gateway of speech. For all this is only so much.
That is to say, whether it be form, action, or name—all that is indeed the heart.
That heart, which consists of all things, is now questioned: "In what, then, is the heart established? //24//
"Ahallika! Yājñavalkya said,
"if you were to think this [Brahman] is somewhere other than in us."
"For if this were anywhere other than with us, dogs would surely eat it, or birds would surely tear it apart. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.25)
"O dullard! Yājñavalkya said;
he addressed him by another name.
At which time—meaning, at that moment—...

You should consider this heart to be the self of this [body], existing as "us" from "us. For if this heart were elsewhere than us, then dogs would surely eat that body, or birds— meaning winged creatures— would tear it apart, mangle it, and scatter it.
Therefore, the meaning is that the heart is established within me, the body;
for since the body itself consists of name, form, and action, it is established in the heart. //25//
Thus, it has been stated that the heart and the body, as well as the effect and the instrument, are established in one another. Therefore, I ask you:
"In what, then, are you and the Self established?"
"It is the out-breath. "On what, then, is the out-breath established?
"It is the in-breath."
"On what, then, is the out-breath (apāna) established? "On the inter-breath (vyāna). "On what, then, is the inter-breath established?"
Regarding "inspiration" (udāna):
upon what is inspiration established?
Upon the "equalizing breath" (samāna).
This very Self is "not this, not this.
It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped; it is indestructible, for it is not destroyed.
Unattached, he is not bound; unseated, he is not distressed;
he does not come to harm.

"These eight bases, these eight worlds, these eight gods, and these eight persons—having projected them forth and withdrawn them back, he passed beyond them. Of that person of the Upaniṣads, I ask you:
if you do not explain him to me, your head shall shatter apart."
Śākalya did not know him;
his head fell apart,
and thieves even carried off his bones, thinking them to be something else.
"In what, then, are you and your body and your self established within the heart?
"In the vital breath (prāṇa). Both the body and the self would be established in the vital breath, that is, in the function of the prāṇa.

"In what, then, are the vital breaths established? "In the downward breath (apāna). For even that function of the prāṇa would depart before its time if it were not held back by the function of the apāna.
"On what, then, is the apāna established?

"On the vyāna. For otherwise, the function of the apāna would simply move downward, and the function of the prāṇa would simply move forward; it is only when they are restrained by the intermediate function of the vyāna that they are held in check.
"On what is the vyāna established? "On the udāna. For if all three modes of movement were not restrained within the udāna, which stands like a wedge, they would simply go in every direction.
"On what is udāna established?
"On samāna"—for all these functions are indeed established upon samāna.
This means that the body, the heart, and the vital airs are mutually dependent.
"They exist as seated together, engaged with objects consisting of consciousness.

This entire [universe], by which it is determined and in which it is established—woven like warp and woof unto the limits of space—is that Brahman, free from all limiting adjuncts, immediate and direct; this [section] is begun for the purpose of providing a description of Him.
This very one—He who was pointed out in the Madhu-kāṇḍa as "not this, not this"—is He. This is that Self; it is ungraspable, for it cannot be grasped.
Why? Because it transcends all qualities of effects.
Therefore, it is ungraspable.
Why? Because it is not grasped.
For that which is within the range of the sense organs is a determinate object; [but this is not so].
That [world] is the object of perception; however, this reality of the Self is the opposite of that.
Likewise, it is indestructible; for whatever is material and composite, such as the body and so forth, that is subject to destruction.
But this [Self] is the opposite of that, and therefore it does not decay.

Likewise, that which is attached and corporeal becomes entangled when connected with another corporeal thing; but this [Self] is the opposite of that, and therefore it is not entangled. Likewise, it is unattached and unbound.
For that which is material is subject to destruction;
however, because this [Self] is the opposite of that and is unbound, it does not suffer.

Therefore, it does not perish—meaning that, being devoid of the properties associated with the effects of grasping and dissolution, it does not perish, does not undergo injury, and does not come to an end.

Having bypassed the sequence and departed from the narrative concerning the Puruṣa of the Upaniṣads, the Śruti has provided a direct description of him in his own form with urgency; then, returning once more to the narrative itself, it says: "These eight abodes which have been mentioned—'the earth is his abode,' and so forth—and the eight worlds, beginning with the world of Agni."
"Eight deities are the immortal," so he said; and likewise,
"Eight persons [make] the person in the body," and so forth.

Whoever has drawn out those persons beginning with the embodied self, having ascertained and internalized them by means of the division into groups of eight and four, thereby establishing the order of the worlds;

and who, having again withdrawn and reabsorbed them through the doors of the eastern direction and so forth, transcended within his own self in the heart—that is, he has passed beyond the attributes of the limiting adjuncts such as having the heart as one's identity—and remains established in his own true self: that person of the Upaniṣads, who is free from hunger and other such needs, who is to be known through the Upaniṣads alone and is not accessible through any other means of knowledge.
"I ask you, that person who presumes his own learning;
if you do not speak clearly to me— that is, if you will not explain it— your head shall shatter," said Yājñavalkya.
Śākalya did not know—that is, he certainly did not understand—that Puruṣa who is described in the Upaniṣads; indeed, his head fell off—meaning it fell down. This concludes the narrative.
The words of Śruti are: "He did not know him," and so forth.
Moreover, even though robbers and thieves stole his bones—even as they were being carried toward his home by a disciple for the purpose of cremation—why did they do so?
Because they thought they were carrying some other kind of wealth.
For a story from the past is indicated here.
It is said that the dialogue between Śākalya and Yājñavalkya concerning the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* ended right at the point of agreement;
thereupon, Yājñavalkya uttered a curse: "You shall die before reaching home as a guest, and neither your bones nor your home shall receive you.
He indeed died exactly so.
Thinking he was asleep, thieves indeed stole his belongings;
therefore, one should not be a detractor, for even one who knows this becomes superior.
This story has been indicated here for the sake of [establishing] right conduct and for the praise of knowledge. //26//
Since Brahman has been indicated by means of the negation of everything else through the formula "not this, not this," how is its indication to be made by way of affirmation?
Thus, once again resorting to a narrative, [the text] says that the root of the world must also be explained.

But the connection of this narrative is as follows: considering it to be the proper course of action, [Nārada] said, "Having conquered the Brahmins who do not know Brahman, their wealth of cattle should be carried away. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.27)
Then he said: "Venerable Brahmins, let whoever among you wishes may question me; or let all of you question me.
Or, let me question whoever among you wishes; or let me question all of you."
Those Brahmins did not dare [to speak].
Then he said:
immediately thereafter, when the Brahmins had become silent, he spoke, addressing them thus: "O venerable Brahmins, whoever among you desires—that is, wishes—to ask Yājñavalkya,"
Let him come to me and question me;
or let all of you question me—let all of you question me!
Whosoever among you desires it, let Yājñavalkya question me.
"I ask that from you";
that is, I am asking all of you.
Those Brahmins did not dare; even though they were addressed in this way, those Brahmins did not become bold enough to say anything by way of reply. //27//
He questioned them with these verses:
"As a tree is a great forest-plant, so indeed is a person— not falsely."
Its hairs are the leaves, and its outer bark is the skin.
When those Brahmins had become disconcerted, he questioned them—that is, he asked them—using these verses which are about to be stated:
"Just as in the world there is a tree, a *vanaspati*"; here, *vanaspati* is a specific epithet for a tree.
In the same way, the person is not false, not false—this is the truth: his body hairs are the body hairs of that person;
the leaves of the other, the tree, are the body hairs of that person. His outer bark is the outer bark of the other, the tree. //1//
From his skin alone flows the blood; it is a scab from the skin.
Therefore, when it is wounded, the sap flows out, just as [sap flows] from a tree that has been struck.
From the skin itself of this person, blood flows out, just as from the bark of a tree a shoot emerges— for it is from the bark itself that it bursts forth;
thus, everything is exactly the same for both the tree and the person.
From that which is pierced and wounded, blood flows out from it, just as sap flows from a tree that has been struck or cut. //2//
The flesh is its shavings;
the sinews are the inner bark; the bones are the inner wood; and the marrow is made like the pith within.
In this way, the flesh belongs to this person; the "śakarāṇi" of the tree mean its splinters or chips;
and the "kināṭam" is the inner bark of the tree.
What is called *kināṭa* is that which is inside the outer bark, a form of inner bark adhering to the wood; that is the sinew (*snāyu*) of a person.
It is firm; for that *kināṭa* is indeed as solid as a sinew.
The bones of a person:
within the sinews there are bones;
likewise, within the inner pith of a tree there are pieces of wood; [and] marrow.
The marrow of the tree and the marrow of the person have been made comparable as "marrow-like" (*majjopamā*); the meaning is that there is no other distinction between the marrow and its comparison.
As is the pith of a tree, so is that of a person; as is that of a person, so is that of a tree. //3//
When a tree is cut down, it grows back again, newer from the root; but when a mortal is cut down by death, from what root does he sprout forth?
If a tree, having been cut down or felled, grows again and again, sprouting anew from the root more fresh than before— more fresh than its previous state— then,
prior to this specific distinction between the tree and the person, everything was understood to be common to both.
But this distinction is observed in the case of a tree: that it sprouts again after being cut down; however, when a person is felled by death, no such sprouting is observed again.
And yet, there must be some source from which sprouting occurs.
Therefore I ask you: from what root does a mortal man, once cut down by death, sprout forth again? The meaning is: from where does the rebirth of a dead person originate? //4//
"Do not say, 'From semen,' for that is produced from one who is living. Like a tree growing from a seed, rebirth after death occurs directly."
If you say that semen sprouts [from the dead], do not say so; you ought not to speak thus. Why?
Because that semen is produced from a living person, not from one who is dead.
Moreover, there is that which grows from a grain; "grain" means a seed,
and thus it is a tree that grows from a seed.
It is not only the stalk that [is reborn];
the word "iva" is meaningless here.
Indeed, a tree, having died, comes into existence directly and immediately; even from a seed, after death, there may be immediate rebirth as a lord of the forest. //5//
Just as a tree that they might uproot together with its roots would not grow again,
from what root does a mortal man, once cut down by death, sprout forth again?
If they were to uproot a tree along with its root—whether by plucking the grain or by pulling it out—it would not come back to life; having returned, it would not exist again.
Therefore I ask you: from what root does the entire world sprout forth when it has been cut down by death? //6//
Already born, he is not born again; who indeed could give birth to him anew?
Consciousness, bliss, Brahman—this is the supreme goal for the giver of gifts. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28:7–8)
He who is already born is not born again; who indeed could give birth to him?
Consciousness, bliss, Brahman—the gift and the supreme goal of the giver.
"For one who stands firm, knowing that. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28)
If you think, "He is indeed born," then what is there to be asked? For it is the birth of one who is not yet born that ought to be questioned, not the birth of one who is already born.
Since this one is indeed born, no question at all is applicable in this regard—if this is your objection, we say: no, why is that?
"The dead would surely be born again, otherwise there would be the consequence of the arrival of what was not done and the loss of what was done.
Therefore, I ask you: who indeed would produce this one who has died?
Thereupon the Brahmins were unable to discern it; they did not know the root of the world from which the dead sprout forth again.
Therefore, because of his supreme devotion to Brahman, the cows were won back;
the Brahmins were defeated by Yājñavalkya.
The narrative is concluded.
That which is the root of the world,
that by which Brahman is directly designated through speech,
and that which Yājñavalkya questioned the Brāhmaṇas— Scripture declares its nature for us: it is consciousness (*vijñāna*), the act of cognizing, consciousness.
And that bliss is not accompanied by suffering as is the case with the cognition of objects; what then?

It means it is serene, auspicious, incomparable, effortless, eternally satisfied, and of a single flavor. What is that Brahman? Like the word *umaya*, it is a compound where the genitive case has the sense of the nominative—that is, it is a gift (*rāti*) from the giver (*rāti*).
The meaning is "of wealth";

He is the ultimate resort (*parāyaṇa*), the supreme goal, and the giver of the fruits of action for the donor of wealth, the performer of rituals, the sacrificer. Furthermore, having withdrawn from all desires, even one who does not perform ritual actions abides in this very Brahman.
"One who knows that" means one who knows Brahman; "of him"—that is, of the knower of Brahman—while he is thus abiding. This is the meaning.

Regarding the term "supreme resort" (*parāyaṇa*): here this is investigated—the word *ānanda* is well-known in the world as denoting happiness, and in this context, the word *ānanda* is heard as a qualification of Brahman, in the passage: "Brahman is bliss" (*ānandaṃ brahma*).

And in another Śruti passage: “He understood that bliss is Brahman”; “Knowing the bliss of Brahman”; “If this bliss did not exist in the ether [of the heart]”; “That which is the Infinite (bhūman), that is happiness”; and “This is the supreme bliss”—such passages as these occur. Furthermore, the word "bliss" (ānanda) is well-known in the sense of a happiness that is experienced; therefore, if the bliss of Brahman were also something to be experienced, these uses of the word "bliss" with respect to Brahman would be appropriate.
But is it not the case that, on the authority of the Vedas, Brahman is of the very nature of bliss that is to be experienced; what, then, remains to be investigated there?
No, for we observe Vedic statements that are contradictory—this is true.

The word "bliss" (ānanda) is heard in reference to Brahman, and there is a negation of cognition regarding unity: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?
By what and whom should he know? "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, knows nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūmā). [And] "by the conscious Self..."
"Being embraced [by the Supreme Self], he knows nothing external," and so forth.
Since such contradictory scriptural statements are observed, an inquiry must be undertaken.
Therefore, it is proper to investigate for the sake of determining the meaning of the Vedic texts.

Furthermore, because there are conflicting views among those who propound liberation: the Sāṃkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas, being proponents of liberation, hold the contrary view that in liberation there is no pleasure to be experienced;
others, however, maintain that there is an unsurpassed pleasure to be personally experienced.
Which of these two positions is, then, the correct one?

Because of scriptural passages such as "bliss" (*ānanda*) and so forth; and from texts like "eating, playing, rejoicing," "if he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers," "he who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," and "he enjoys all desires," it follows that in liberation (*mokṣa*), happiness is something to be experienced.
[Objection: But if there is oneness, the impossibility of cognition arises because of the absence of the distinction between the factors of action (*kāraka-vibhāga*).
And since an action is accomplished by multiple factors (kārakas), and cognition is itself an action,
this is not a fault;
for through the authority of scripture, there may be cognition regarding the object that is bliss.
We have already stated that such statements as "Consciousness is bliss" would be untenable if the nature of bliss were something incapable of being experienced.
Now, one might object: even by means of a verbal statement, the coldness of fire or the heat of water is certainly not produced, for words function only as indicators.
Nor can it be made known that fire is cold in another place,
or that water is warm in an inaccessible region;
[this is not so], because bliss and consciousness are perceived within one's own self.
Statements such as "consciousness is bliss" do not, like sentences such as "fire is cold," convey a meaning that contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition;
rather, their non-contradictory nature is experienced,
for one personally perceives the self as consisting of bliss in the form, "I am happy."
Therefore, its meaning is all the more consistent with perception;
thus, Brahman, being bliss and consisting of consciousness, experiences itself by its own nature.
In this way, the scriptural passages establishing bliss—such as those previously mentioned beginning with "eating, playing, and rejoicing"—would be rendered coherent.
No, for consciousness is impossible in the absence of an effect-producing instrument; indeed, liberation is the absolute dissociation from the body,
and as long as the body exists, the instrument [of cognition] is impossible due to the absence of a substratum.

Consequently, consciousness would not arise, because it lacks a body and its instruments; and if consciousness were to arise in the absence of the body and so forth, it would follow that the acquisition of all bodies and instruments is purposeless.

Furthermore, because of the contradiction with oneness: if the Supreme Brahman, being of the nature of bliss, were to know itself eternally due to its nature as eternal consciousness, that would not be so;
for even the transmigrating soul would then attain its true nature, being already liberated from transmigratory existence.
Just as a handful of water thrown into a reservoir does not remain separate from it, so too for the sake of realizing Brahman whose nature is bliss,

the statement that "the liberated one experiences the Self whose nature is bliss" would be meaningless. Alternatively, if the liberated one experiences the bliss of Brahman while being something other than it, [then the same fault follows].
And [the realization] "I am the inner self whose nature is bliss"— there is a contradiction between these two regarding their oneness.
And this being the case, there would be a contradiction with all the scriptures,
and the third alternative is not tenable.
Furthermore, if Brahman consists of an uninterrupted self-bliss and consciousness, the conceptualization of "knowledge" and "non-knowledge" would be purposeless.

If the cognition of Brahman were continuously directed toward the object that is self-bliss, then that [bliss] would be its very nature; thus, the conceptualization that "it cognizes self-bliss" is untenable.
For a conceptualization is meaningful only when there is the possibility of cognizing something other than that [inherent nature].
As for the claim that one knows both oneself and another, this is not the case;
for one whose mind is attached to arrows and the like, the conceptualization of continuous knowledge or non-knowledge of the arrow lacks purpose.
Furthermore, if one perceives the bliss of the Self as something interrupted, it would follow that during the gaps in the knowledge of the Self, consciousness must have other objects as its domain.
Furthermore, [if the Self were subject to modification], it would possess the quality of transformation, and from that would follow the consequence of its impermanence;

therefore, the scriptural statement "Bliss is consciousness" is intended solely as a description of the Self's essential nature, not for the purpose of establishing that bliss is an object of the Self's cognition.
If it is argued that there is a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "eating and playing," because [liberation] would then involve being conscious [of these acts], we say no;

for when there is the oneness of the Self of all, the text merely restates what is already established. When the liberated one has attained the state of being the Self of all, whatever eating and so forth occurs—whether among yogis or among the gods—is simply restated as it is found to occur, because he is the Self of all. This is for the purpose of praising liberation as the state of being the Self of all.

If it is argued that, just as [the Lord] merely restates what has been obtained, He must likewise experience suffering—just as He experiences hunger and so forth in the case of the *yogīs* and others, so too must He experience suffering as it occurs in the case of stationary beings (*sthāvara*) and the like—we say:

no. This entire point has already been refuted, because the distinctions such as being happy or being miserable are merely superimposed through the error produced by contact with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the body and organs (*kāryakaraṇa*) formed by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Furthermore, we have already explained the scope of the apparently contradictory scriptural passages.
Therefore, all statements concerning bliss should be understood in the same manner as the statement: "This is his supreme bliss. //28//
Thus ends the ninth Śākalya Brāhmaṇa in the third chapter.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. //3//
